#5640. Massachusetts Plan for More Starter Homes Fails as ‘NIMBY’ Voters Insist on Local Zoning Control

Massachusetts voters rejected Question 7, a ballot initiative aimed at promoting starter homes by reducing the size of the lot required to build a home.

The initiative would have established a new minimum lot size of 5,000 square feet for single-family homes. The lot would need at least 50 feet of land bordering the street or public way, and it would also need access to public sewer and water, but otherwise, it would pave the way for smaller starter homes to be built across Massachusetts.

The measure failed by a slim margin of 50.6% to 49.4%.

"I think that, you know, there unfortunately is still a lot of NIMBYism throughout Massachusetts," says Mike Travaline, the government affairs chair of the Homebuilders and Remodelers Association of Massachusetts. The HBRA supported the measure, arguing that it would help address the state's 220,000-home shortage and allow builders to build more starter homes.

"There's a lot of resistance to any type of legislation or referendum that would take away local control from each individual municipality," he tells Realtor.com®. "Residents and town politicians really want to have the final say in what gets built in their towns."

Massachusetts has a serious lack of smaller, more affordable starter homes, which is preventing young residents from becoming homebuyers and keeping older residents locked into larger homes they can no longer afford to keep up.

The lack of starter homes in the state is part of an overall national trend away from smaller homes. The median home size in the 1960s was 1,500 square feet. By 2024, the median home size had grown to 2,205 square feet.

A Tufts University study found that approving Question 7 could create between 3,500 and 12,000 net new homes in its first decade and ultimately increase Massachusetts' housing supply by up to 320,000 units.

Andrew Mikula, the ballot initiative's organizer and chief housing economist at the Pioneer Institute, spearheaded the effort.

"We're grateful to have the support of more than 1.2 million voters who support bringing more starter homes to families across Massachusetts," he tells Realtor.com.

Currently, lot minimums are determined at the local level. A zoning report from the National Zoning Atlas found that over half the municipalities in the state require lots to be a minimum of 40,000 square feet—or about an acre—to build a home.

Those restrictive zoning laws are part of why Massachusetts received an "F" grade and was ranked almost dead last in the Realtor.com Affordability and Homebuilding Report Card two years in a row. The state was dinged for its complex zoning rules, along with its high prices, and high construction costs.

Massachusetts' median listing price is $699,990, around $250,000 more than the national median listing price of $415,000.

"From a developer perspective, we know that if we if we did build it, they will come," Travaline says.

"There's just gigantic pent up demand for that type of housing in Massachusetts because that housing really just does not exist in any sort of substantive quantity," he continues. "We don't have enough small homes that would appeal to first time homebuyers or young professionals, young families or empty nesters."

Travaline believes the bill was defeated because of pushback from local politicians who "really want to have the final say in what gets built in their towns."

Indeed, that was a major point of contention, according to Adam Chapdelaine of the Massachusetts Municipal Association, which opposed the measure. Chapdelaine wrote in an op-ed that the proposed zoning law would "override local planning" and replace "thoughtful local planning with a one-size-fits-all mandate that ignores the individual needs of all 351 Massachusetts cities and towns."

Travaline says that many towns are concerned about how the passage of Question 7 might impact housing density.

But from his perspective, "it gives developers another alternative when they're buying a lot. Rather than maybe taking the risk that they have to build a really large single-family home on a lot in order to make their return that might have to sell for you know, $1.8 to $2.5 million, they could instead create two or three smaller homes on that lot and still make their return."

"Massachusetts residents, especially young people, are leaving the state to find a more affordable place to live, separating extended families and hurting our economy," Wesley Lima, of Legalize Starter Homes, wrote in an op-ed. "Requiring huge lot sizes to build a single family home makes houses expensive, reduces construction of new single-family housing, and encourages developers to build giant McMansions to recoup land costs. Anyone who needs a low-cost, single-family suburban home is all but locked out of the market."

Mikula says his next step is to "get into all the demographic data and kind of assess you know, where where we think, you know, policies like this can pass and then go from there."

#5638. SmartMLS Introduces New Ownership Verification Tool to Help Combat Seller-Impersonation and Land Scams

With security and insurance symbols prominently featured, the property house cautioned against falling victim to scammers and fraud.

Connecticut’s SmartMLS has announced that it will introduce a new Ownership Verification tool from Property Shield designed to help real estate professionals combat seller-impersonation and vacant-land scams.

According to a release, the new technology, expected to become available to SmartMLS next week, provides an additional way for real estate professionals to verify the identity of someone claiming to own a property before accepting a listing.

Seller-impersonation fraud typically begins when a scammer poses as a property owner and contacts a real estate professional seeking to list and sell property the scammer does not own. These schemes can be particularly difficult to identify when the property is vacant land or when the purported seller communicates remotely.

“Seller-impersonation scams can be difficult to identify.” said Kathy Elson, CEO of SmartMLS. “We want to give our users a tool to help verify a prospective seller’s identity and identify a potential problem as early in the listing process as possible.”

An additional step when something doesn’t look right

Property Shield’s Ownership Verification tool is designed to help determine whether the individual claiming to be the property owner is who they say they are.

The verification process uses identity verification and facial-recognition technology in conjunction with property ownership information to provide an additional layer of protection when questions arise about the identity of a prospective seller.

Rather than relying solely on documents, emails, telephone conversations, or information supplied by the prospective seller, real estate professionals will have a tool available to help evaluate whether the person attempting to list the property is legitimate.

“Real estate professionals are often on the front line when seller-impersonation fraud is attempted,” Elson said. “The challenge is that a sophisticated scammer may have enough information about the property and its owner to appear legitimate. Ownership Verification gives our users another way to ask an important question before proceeding: Is this really the property owner?”

Helping stop fraud before a listing enters the MLS

Ownership Verification complements the Listing Fraud Protection technology SmartMLS has already introduced through its partnership with Property Shield.

The two technologies address fraud at different points.

Listing Fraud Protection helps identify when legitimate SmartMLS listing information is copied and used in potentially fraudulent advertisements across the web.

Ownership Verification is designed to help identify potential seller impersonation before a fraudulent listing enters the MLS.

Together, the tools provide SmartMLS users with additional ways to identify and respond to real estate fraud.

“Seller impersonation and vacant-land fraud are difficult problems because the person committing the fraud may never meet the agent face-to-face,” said Alexander Fahsel, CEO of Property Shield. “Ownership Verification gives real estate professionals another layer of information to help determine whether the person they are dealing with is actually connected to the property they are attempting to sell.”

Technology supporting professional judgment

Ownership Verification is intended to provide an additional fraud-prevention tool, not replace the judgment and due diligence of the real estate professional.

A successful verification should not eliminate other appropriate steps when circumstances surrounding a prospective listing raise concerns. Similarly, an issue identified during verification can provide an important signal that additional investigation may be warranted before proceeding with the listing.

“Our goal isn’t to replace the due diligence brokers and agents already perform,” Elson said. “It’s to give them a better tool when they need it. If something about a prospective seller or listing doesn’t add up, we want our users to have another way to investigate before moving forward.”

For more information, visit smartmls.com and propertyshield.co.

#5637. Cloudflare shares surge as revenue growth accelerates to 39% and outlook rises

Shares of Cloudflare Inc. jumped more than 14% in late trading today after the connectivity cloud company smashed third-quarter expectations and lifted its full-year outlook well above what Wall Street had been modeling.

The gain more than wiped out an 8% fall in the stock during the regular session.

For the quarter ended on Sept. 30, Cloudflare reported adjusted earnings per share of 38 cents, up from 27 cents in the same quarter of 2025, on revenue of $782.5 million, up 39% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of 34 cents per share on revenue of $736.8 million.

Revenue growth hit its fastest pace in nearly four years as the annualized run rate crossed $3 billion. Current remaining performance obligations rose 37% from a year earlier. The adjusted operating margin also improved, to 17.5% from 15.3%, after shrinking year-over-year in each of the two prior quarters.

Because stock-based compensation ran to $174.1 million, Cloudflare still lost $34.1 million on an unadjusted basis, compared with a $1.3 million loss a year earlier. Another $11 million went to restructuring from the roughly 1,100 job cuts announced in May. Free cash flow slipped to 10% of revenue from 13% a year ago.

On the product side, short-lived blocking rules that write themselves during a live attack are the core of Adaptive Intelligence, which Cloudflare added to its Bot Management product in late August. AI agents got tools of their own earlier in the month through Cloudflare Wallets and cloudflare.pay, which give an agent an identity handle and will let it pay for services from a stablecoin balance. Federal agencies can now put more sensitive workloads on Cloudflare for Government, which reached FedRAMP High status in August.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Matthew Prince called the period “Cloudflare’s best quarter ever” in the earnings release. Cloudflare has built the development platform for the AI-powered internet, and organizations of every size keep turning to it for protection as digital threats escalate, he said. Prince added that the business has “found an even higher gear for this next phase of growth.”

Cloudflare also named Christian Smith president of revenue today, with responsibility for worldwide sales and revenue operations. He replaces Mark Anderson, who had already said he would retire from the full-time role at year-end. Smith previously ran sales at Splunk Inc. as chief revenue officer.

For the fourth quarter, Cloudflare expects adjusted earnings of 43 cents per share on revenue of $845 million to $846 million. Analysts had forecast 38 cents per share on revenue of $798.2 million.

Cloudflare now expects 2026 revenue of $2.963 billion to $2.964 billion, about $97 million above the midpoint of the range it gave in August. Analysts had been looking for $2.87 billion in revenue and $1.26 in adjusted earnings per share for the year, and the company is now guiding to $1.35.

#5636. California Passes Down Payment Assistance Plan, but Push To Cut Red Tape Remains in Limbo

California voters headed to the polls on Tuesday to decide three new housing-related ballot measures. While two of them handily passed, votes are still being counted on a plan to cut red tape and streamline environmental reviews for new homes.

Voters approved Proposition 1, which authorizes California to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, permanent supportive housing, and affordable housing. The funding also backs both down payment assistance programs and mortgage programs for veterans.

Gov. Gavin Newsom expressed support for the measure, as did the Democratic Party of California. The ACLU, the California Apartment Association, and the California Housing Consortium also supported the measure, although there was some scattered opposition from Republican state legislators.

"This bond is about building communities, expanding access and affordability in California, where every family has a fair shot at a place to call home," Newsom said in a June statement.

Voters backed a similar measure in 2024 that earmarked $6.38 billion for homelessness and veterans housing programs.

"Higher mortgage rates have squeezed homebuyers and the for-sale market for four years, and they have hurt builders, too, especially in multifamily," Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner says.

"Apartment projects depend on layers of financing, and assembling it has gotten much harder at today’s borrowing costs, particularly in a state as expensive and complicated to build in as California. When rates jumped in 2022 and 2023, a backlog of [COVID-19] pandemic-era projects that were already financed kept delivering homes. That backlog has been worked through, and the multifamily pipeline behind it is much thinner today," Berner adds.

Berner calls Prop 1 a "modest attempt to plug this gap" but only "one piece of the puzzle," noting that the infusion of cash won't do much to reduce approval times or land acquisition costs.

Californians also approved Proposition 37, which creates a $25 billion loan program for middle-income earners to purchase new homes. The state would issue bonds and use the proceeds to offer fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of the purchase price of newly constructed homes priced below $1.5 million

Borrowers must be California residents who pay at least 3% down and meet some income requirements. This, supporters say, would help lower the amount they'd need to save for a down payment on a new home. They expect the measure to spur the construction of new homes and be paid for when investors and home borrowers repay the loans.

The California Association of Realtors and the California Chamber of Commerce both supported the measure.

"Voters in California have seized the opportunity to help alleviate the burden of current mortgage rates on new-home buyers," says Berner of the initiative's passage. "With current mortgage rates holding above 7%, this presents the opportunity for buyers to save on interest payments for part of their home purchase, which could be a boon to the new-home segment of sales in the Golden State."

But, says Berner, housing is still above $1.5 million in many California metros, signaling that the measure's impact may be circumscribed.

"The median listing price for newly built single-family homes in the San Jose metro is over $2.1 million. In Los Angeles, it’s over $1.7 million. San Francisco has a median of about $1.5 million, and San Diego’s median is about $1.3 million. Among newly built single-family homes for sale in 2026 in the San Jose metro, just 41.7% were priced below $1.5 million. In Los Angeles, the share was 41.7% as well; 49.5% of newly built single-family homes in San Francisco were below the threshold; and in San Diego, 61.4% were. Proposition 37 has the potential to help prospective California homebuyers, but only if they can find new homes to buy."

Proposition 45 limits timelines on environmental reviews for some projects under the California Environmental Quality Act. These new requirements would expedite environmental review and court challenges to projects.

Votes for the measure are still being counted. With 65% of the votes counted on Friday, 54.9% of Californians have voted against it while 45.1% voted in favor.

Affordable housing advocates—including the Associated General Contractors of California, the California Building Industry Association, the California Council for Affordable Housing, and the California Chamber of Commerce—expressed support for the measure.

Environmental groups and labor unions widely opposed it, arguing that it would reduce environmental oversight and community decision making around new development.

#5635. Bear Grylls Bought a ‘Derelict’ Island With ‘No Power’ and ‘Rats’ at 25 Instead of a London Apartment—Here’s How It Looks Decades Later

Bear Grylls made an unusual decision decades ago, when he acquired a marital starter home with his wife, Shara Grylls.

“At 25, just married, we bought a small, abandoned, off-grid island from an ad in the back of a magazine,” the British adventurer, 52, wrote in a Nov. 3 Instagram caption.

Grylls revealed that the purchase of St. Tudwal’s Island West cost them around $120,000.

“There were many who thought us crazy,” he continued. “The best adventures start with nay-sayers. Thank you Shara for being brave and saying yes!”

While the comment section had users divided over the relatability of purchasing an entire island—with one commenter wondering how “celebrities get so far out of touch from reality and regular people”—there were also a handful of people who stepped in to point out that even when adjusted for inflation, the island was less costly than the average U.S. home.

The “Running Wild With Bear Grylls” star explained the decision to the Sunday Times in 2021, noting that snapping up a Welsh island seemed like a more exciting use of the couple’s money.

“In 2001, we were going to buy a London flat for $288,000, but we bought a houseboat on the Thames [now sold] and the island together, and it cost less than the apartment. So we decided on the path less trodden and an amazing adventure,” he said.

Grylls shed some light on just how dilapidated the property was 25 years ago.

“The island had a 200-year-old lighthouse and two lightkeeper’s cottages, but [the houses] were derelict with no power, no water, no roof, and rats,” he said. “I remember my first bath sitting in 3 inches of water pumped from the old tanks we’d cleaned out. There was rubble everywhere and rain coming through, but it was a great moment.”

Considering Grylls has made a career out of his ability to survive in extremely harsh conditions, it’s not entirely surprising that he was able to get through a few rough years before the island would become a more suitable dwelling.

It took a decade to get permission to build a slipway, which Grylls said they finished just a few years ago.

“It has been life-changing for us,” he said of the addition. “Previously we had to keep a boat on a mooring, row ashore, and walk a mile up the beach with all the shopping.”

Eventually, the two lightkeeper’s cottages were combined into a single home with four bedrooms. But the island is still off-grid.

“It’s 20 acres and 5 miles offshore with no mains, electricity, or running water,” Grylls told Vanity Fair in 2012. “It has a little lighthouse beside our house and is surrounded by amazing sea cliffs, seals, and dolphins. It is my favorite place on the planet!”

To travel to the destination, Grylls and his family take a “30-foot, high-speed ex-lifeboat,” which he described as a “rigid inflatable boat with twin 300-horsepower engines behind it that can tackle any sea it needs to.”

He said the house is “as tough as you get.” Thanks to “2-foot-thick old limestone walls,” it retains heat in the winter and stays cool in the summer.

“But when those gales come in, you can still feel it almost shake,” Grylls admitted. “Sea spray reaches the windows despite the 150-foot elevation.”

While St. Tudwal’s may lack some of the modern amenities guests might typically expect, the Grylls family does “sometimes have friends” visit.

“They need to be up for an adventure and prepared to get stuck there if the weather turns,” he said.

Grylls has recently made headlines for his connection to disgraced former comic Russell Brand, who was recently found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Grylls helped baptize Brand in a ceremony in the River Thames in 2024, after the allegations against the actor had come to light. Prior to the baptism, Brand appeared in a 2023 episode of Grylls’ show, in which the pair traveled across the Hebrides Islands.

“Brand’s faith seemed genuine to me at the time when I was a guest at his private baptism,” Grylls wrote in a Nov. 6 X post. “I have attended a few now. Even visiting in prisons with people who have committed terrible crimes. It’s part of our calling as men and women of faith, to love and serve anyone. It is the sick that need healing.”

Noting that “judgment is for the courts and God,” Grylls added that “it is right that justice has now been served.

“I can’t imagine how hard this time has been for the victims, the heroes of the day,” he said.

#5632. Kourtney Kardashian Slams ‘Fabricated’ Rumors That She Doesn’t Live With Travis Barker and Shares ‘Really Vulnerable’ Renovation of Calabasas Home

Kourtney Kardashian is setting the record straight on her living arrangements with her husband, Travis Barker.

On the Nov. 5 episode of "The Kardashians," the Poosh founder is seen driving around town with her close friend Simon Huck. She mentions that she received a phone call from her publicist, asking her to comment on previous speculation that Kardashian and the Blink-182 drummer were living separately and planning to split.

Kardashian called the claims "speculated rumors."

"I go, 'Tell them to print it. See what happens,'" she recalled.

"I was just like, 'They know it's not true. They know they saw a dumb TikTok of someone who makes up fabricated stories,'" Kardashian continued.

Huck agreed, noting he often sees "crazy, weird conspiracy theories" about Kardashian and her famous family.

"People believe it," Kardashian said of the gossip, which is sometimes fueled by AI-generated clips. It is "so bizarre."

Moments later, Kardashian, Huck, and her stepson, Landon Barker, pulled up to her longtime Calabasas home, which is undergoing a major renovation.

In the scene, Kardashian said she expected they were about six months away from being able to move back in. But she was beginning to second-guess that timeline after seeing how few changes had been made since her last visit.

"It's a really vulnerable feeling to have all of the walls of your home ripped apart. There's no electrical. There's nothing," she said in a confessional interview during the episode. "It's like a very vulnerable feeling."

While the renovation was in too early a stage to gather much about Kardashian's design plans, she did bring the cameras through a guest room that she said was going to be for Landon, before he moved into a place of his own.

The 23-year-old rapper was quick to pipe up and claim the space, however, saying that he'd love to have his own space because his current residence is a rental.

Barker and Kardashian have a large blended family of seven children. In November 2023, they welcomed a son, Rocky Thirteen Barker. Before their marriage in 2022, Kardashian had three children with her ex Scott Disick: Mason Disick, 16, Penelope Disick, 14, and Reign Disick, 11.

In addition to Landon, Barker and his ex Shanna Moakler are parents to a 20-year-old daughter, Alabama Barker. The musician also has a stepdaughter—Atiana De La Hoya, 27, whom Moakler had with boxer Oscar De La Hoya.

When asked if she was planning to house the couple's entire family under one roof, Kardashian appeared to have mixed feelings.

"I love it in theory, but I think it's really hard with everybody of all different ages," she said. "It's a much different balance."

Although all of the children may not end up living in the home full time, Kardashian confirmed there will be plenty of space for everyone to make memories in one way or another.

"We're working toward something amazing," she said. "I can't wait to cook and have movie nights, barbecues. I want to make it feel magical for everybody. It's so fun."

Kardashian and Barker have previously opened up about the arrangements they've made to suit their large family. In a 2024 episode of "The Kardashians," which was filmed when she was pregnant with Rocky in 2023, she discussed their plans to move into Barker's nearby Calabasas estate.

"We're going to move into his house, which is a block away, and then redo my house at the same time so that we can all be together, living under one roof with the baby," she said.

Barker opened the doors of that very house to Architectural Digest in May 2022, revealing a surprisingly laid-back aesthetic for a rocker whose vibe typically leans much edgier.

"I've had homes with lots of flashy cars, murals, and bikes hanging from the ceiling. But with three children of my own, plus Kourtney's kids, this place felt right for this moment in my life," he said. "I wanted a house where I can rest and enjoy my family, a place where we can create memories."

#5631. OpenAI makes new data center commitments, AI policy recommendations

OpenAI Group PBC today made a set of commitments designed to ensure that its data centers benefit the communities where they’re built.

It also proposed that lawmakers make some of the commitments mandatory for artificial intelligence companies.

The move comes two days after Democrats won both the House and the Senate on a campaign backing data center construction curbs. Additionally, voters approved dozens of ballot measures designed to scale back or limit AI infrastructure projects.

OpenAI today reiterated a commitment it made in January to fully pay for the electricity and grid upgrades that its data centers require. That covers items such as the construction of new overhead power lines. Additionally, the company pledged to provide “financial assurances” that will protect other grid users from potential project cancellations and delays.

It will also take steps to reduce grid strain. In particular, it will scale back its data centers’ power draw at times when energy demand is particularly high. That approach, which is known as a flexible data center model, has also drawn the interest of other industry players as Nvidia Corp. and Google LLC.

Some data center builders sign non-disclosure agreements with local officials to keep construction details under wraps. OpenAI today pledged not to use NDAs. It will instead only seek “narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.”

OpenAI will publicly share construction plans and noise projections before construction of a new facility begins. Additionally, it will provide information about the jobs that each data center is expected to create. The goal is to help local unions and training providers prepare residents for the positions.

The company plans to tailor its commitments to each data center. It will publish the customized project terms in a document it calls a local compact. Once construction is underway, the company will provide annual updates and designate a local contact to field residents’ questions.

OpenAI hopes to codify some of the best practices that it published today into law. It released a policy paper that calls on lawmakers to limit data center developers’ use of NDAs and require them to cover their electricity costs. Furthermore, it argues that AI companies should be offered incentives to lower their power usage at times of peak grid stress.

Some of the best practices that the ChatGPT developer is prompting are already being adopted by other industry players. Google, for example, today pledged to fully cover the electricity costs of a new $17 billion data center that it plans to build in Wyoming. It will also finance related grid upgrades. Anthropic PBC made a similar commitment in February.

#5630. Jobs Jump in October, With Unemployment Dipping Slightly

A day after the stock market hit the skids big-time, there was good news on the employment front. U.S. employers hired at a vigorous pace in October, adding 165,000 jobs, way above the 65,000 forecast, while the unemployment rate lowered slightly to 4.1% from 4.2%.

The report from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics shows that employers are continuing to hire workers even with the Iran War raising energy prices, tariffs a continual worry and the uncertainty of how AI will affect businesses on many levels.

The total nonfarm payroll rise of 165,000 jobs is higher than the average monthly gain of 48,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment increased in professional and business services, in healthcare and in transportation and warehousing.

“Today’s report was impressive,” said Realtor.com® Senior Economist Jake Krimmel. “Coming in, we would have been happy with the forecasted 65,000, more than double last month’s. Instead we got more than double. Revisions added another 84,000 jobs to August and September, lifting the three-month average to 137,000 from about 51,000 a month ago.

“This is still a low hire, low fire market overall, but we could be seeing some green shoots on the hiring side. The numbers could still be revised, of course, and the trend matters more than any one point; but you don’t get a good trend without a good month.”

The report might be a welcome sign for the broader economy one day after stocks plummeted, with AI-centric companies hit hardest. For housing markets, though, the stability comes with a caveat—inflation is likely more of a primary concern for policymakers.

Krimmel noted that for the Fed, the report clears the way for a rate hike, because a soft jobs report was the one thing that could have complicated December.

“If Fed hawks were waiting to exhale, they can do so now,” he said. “One question that keeps coming up is whether the midterms changed anything for the housing market. In the short run, not much—the Iran War and its impact on inflation and mortgage rates remain the major wildcard. Getting back to ‘normal’ in many metros takes more activity, which depends on improved buying power to bring buyers off the sidelines.”

Krimmel noted that mortgage rates have declined for three straight weeks after a massive 74 basis point surge from late August to mid-October, but wages are the other half of buying power.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5628. Opendoor Says It ‘Rebuilt’ System With AI, Triples Home Purchases

After over a year of working as CEO, Opendoor’s Kaz Nejatian reported significant growth in revenue and market share during the iBuyer’s Q3 earnings call, and attributed the gains to a shift into AI infrastructure as the company says it has found ways to flip more homes without overpaying.

“This past quarter we rebuilt this entire system at Opendoor. We built an AI system that determines a specific repair plan for every single home before we buy it,” he stated. “Until August, our resale process was similar to literally everyone else in real estate. Pricing every home we owned basically lived in glorified spreadsheets with over 70 columns.”

As real estate incumbents have largely moved on from the iBuying craze that swept over the pandemic boom market, Opendoor has continued to push forward with a more nuanced approach to the model, offering a wider array of services to home sellers and partnerships with agents.

While acknowledging the company still has a long way to go, Nejatian is claiming the turnaround is working, even amid what he characterized as the worst years for housing “in a long time.”

“We’re winning the market without having to make riskier offers,” he said.

A lot of that comes from technology, along with a stronger focus on moving homes faster with less investment. Nejatian pointed out the differences between scaling with employees than with technology. He stated that increasing scale with the traditional method of buying homes involved hiring more employees, and a longer process.

“Rather than having people spending their days looking at pictures and doing mundane tasks, our people now each manage an army of agents,” he added. “In July, we had 5,400 homes. That’s 5,400 sellers sitting in a queue waiting for days for a human to confirm the price on their home. Two weeks ago, that queue was zero, and it will remain zero.”

He also homed in on the iBuyer’s new initiative—Buy with Opendoor—which launched in beta earlier this week. Although the Q3 earnings predates the program’s release, Opendoor CFO Christy Schwartz believes the initiative can open the company up to the broader market.

“Our emerging Buy with Opendoor offering can help buyers whether or not they’re buying a home from Opendoor,” she noted. “We see an opportunity to extend title and escrow to customers who aren’t buying or selling through Opendoor. Similar to listings, the offerings extend our reach beyond our home acquisition business and create opportunities to earn without taking ownership of a home.”

Previously, Nejatian came into the role with an aggressive turnaround mindset, touting an “Opendoor 2.0” initiative to bring the company back to significant profitability. The third quarter earnings may reflect the fruits of his labor, as homes purchased more than quadrupled.

“When a market slows down, companies are left with a cost structure and a system built for a different business. That’s the disease that Opendoor 2.0 is designed to cure,” he added. “That’s why I spend so much of my time on these calls talking about operator efficiency. When we say we’re investing in growth, we are building the capacity to handle the growth that will arrive.”

Overall, Opendoor’s third quarter saw a revenue of $1.02 billion, up 12% from last year’s revenue of $915 million and up 16% from the previous quarter of $883 million.

The number of homes purchased skyrocketed as well, increasing by 316% year-over-year from 1,169 in 2025 to 4,865 in 2026.

At the same time, though, Nejatian acknowledged the company is “behind schedule” on reaching profitability by the end of the year, blaming the slow market.

Opendoor’s stock fell sharply after the report, down about 17% at press time.

Again, Nejatian posited that the increases in efficiency with AI infrastructure have contributed to Q3’s results.

“Not that long ago, around 80% of the assessments we did on homes required an Opendoor employee, which could take many weeks. Today, that 80% is 2%,” he said. “In Q3, we purchased more than four times as many homes as a year ago, and our operation expense was basically the same.”

Operation expenses per acquired home fell to $4,000, down 36% from last year’s expenses of $6,300. The marketing expenses per acquired home dropped at a higher rate, down 57% to $2,800, compared to 2025’s $6,500.

Mortgage originations—or the process in which a borrower goes through to receive a home loan—increased over 400% from quarter-to-quarter, although the Q3 earnings may not reflect the full weight of the Federal Reserve’s rate hike in mid-September. While the latest data does show mortgage rates inching down slowly each week, it’s unclear as to when rates will go below 7%.

“Historically, most of our economics have come from buying and reselling homes complimented by title and escrow,” Schwartz described. “Our emerging mortgage offerings allow us to earn more from each relationship while meeting a critical customer need and making the transaction easier.”

Opendoor’s EBITDA loss also improved slightly on a yearly basis. Q3 2026 had an EBITDA loss of $31 million, while last year had an EBITDA of $33 million. The adjusted EBITDA margin also decreased, now at 3% compared to last year’s margin of 3.6%. While better than last year, Schwartz acknowledged that the latest data is still far off from last quarter’s EBITDA loss of $4 million.

“Most of the sequential decline came from the homes we bought in the spring selling into a much weaker market along with deeper price cuts as we chose to clear rather than hold,” she said.

Looking to the future, Schwartz expects margins to decline again in the fourth quarter, and states that they will continue to sell through the remaining spring acquisitions into Q1 2027.

She also expects revenue to grow by at least 40% on a yearly basis in the next quarter. Although revenue may increase, Schwartz noted that marketing does contain a seasonal aspect, and operating expenses will likely increase due to investments and growth.

“Comparing year-over-year, roughly a third of the increase in our expected loss is the additional marketing, and the remaining two-thirds is primarily higher holding costs as we’ve been rebuilding our inventory,” she concluded.

“Our goal is to be adjusted net income positive on a 12-month-forward basis at the end of this year,” Nejatian continued. “We’re a bit behind on this today, but we’re going to go through some walls and catch up.”

#5626. ‘We Started Buying Real Estate To Help Those in Need—and Built a Portfolio Worth Millions in the Process’

When Frank and Ann Ewing decided to purchase a rundown property in West Tennessee to renovate and rent out, they did so with the idea that they wanted to help provide affordable housing for others. What they didn't expect was that they'd also become millionaires in the process.

But that's exactly what happened as the Ewings quietly built a real estate portfolio over the past 20 years that's now worth around $10 million, while simultaneously making a small dent in the housing affordability crisis in their area.

"We decided that many of the world's problems start at home—all people deserve a safe, decent place to live and a lack of a decent place to live can cause social problems that affect us all," says Ann Ewing, the co-founder, with her husband, of Better World Enterprises and co-author of "Housing Into Homes," which illustrates how it's possible to make money in real estate while "doing good" at the same time.

Step by step, the Ewings amassed not only an entire portfolio of properties including a 33-unit townhouse complex, 20 duplexes, and single-family homes (about 90 rental units in total), but they stayed true to their initial mission, which was to help make the world a better place.

When Frank and Ann first met through an online dating site in the fall of 2000, they both lived in the Northeast. Their connection was immediate and their shared life goals aligned to the point that getting married in August 2001 felt like an easy decision.

During the time they were dating, however, Frank's mother tragically passed away. Though she'd been ill for some time, it was still a tough transition, but one they weathered as a couple. And in the process, they inherited a home in Jackson, TN. After the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, the couple decided to leave New York, where they'd been living, and move down south.

Once in Jackson, the Ewings "took some time to learn about Jackson, and learned that, at that time, West Tennessee was the bankruptcy capital of the world." As such, they realized they were actually in the perfect place to begin their Better World Project.

The couple planned to combine Ann's business acumen (she's a Dartmouth and Wharton School of Business alum) with Frank's expertise in home restoration, repairs, and improvements to make their dream come to life. And by 2002, they had started doing business as Better World Properties.

It was word of mouth that helped the Ewings find their first property to purchase in Jackson.

"We became aware of a somewhat neglected two-bedroom, one-bathroom home in a good neighborhood near our city's largest hospital and decided to check it out," says Ann. "We bought it, cleaned it up, and promptly rented it [out]."

They used some money they'd saved to purchase that first property for $55,000 (this was in 2002, so home prices were more accessible), and decided to rent it out for $550/month. The rent calculation was based on 1% of the investment property.

"As properties that are not in good condition sell for less than better maintained properties, and since we did much of the work on the property ourselves, we were able to rent it [out] for a bit below the standard rental rate in the area and still cover our costs," says Ann. ""The numbers meant that our investment should generate roughly a 10% return per year, not including the increased value of the property or tax benefits."

Today, after eventually adding an additional bathroom and bedroom, that first property is worth over $200,000.

Though it was personal savings that financed their first home acquisition, once they'd made that purchase they were able to use the collateral from that first home to purchase their second property—a neglected four-plex that had been constructed in 1938.

It needed significant work, much of which they did themselves again, including sanding all the wood floors and repainting the premises. But after purchasing it for $53,400 and restoring it to its original elegance, they had every unit rented out right away.

"We rented it [out] at rates ranging from $450 to $900 from 2002 to 2023 ... and in the process, we turned a 'dump' into a beautiful building," explain the Ewings. "It was hard work, but very rewarding psychologically as well as financially."

The calculations the Ewings use to determine what they rent their properties for include variables beyond simply making a profit. But in the balance, they also found themselves coming out ahead, which in turn allowed them to continue the process of buying, renovating, and renting to tenants.

"It is cheaper and quicker for an investor to buy a property that needs attention—everything from a little cleanup to a major renovation, bring it to good condition, and rent it out rather than tear it down and build a new property with new materials," says Ann. "Therefore, since housing is available to the community faster, and with a quicker return on investment, the owner can still make a profit while accepting a lower rent."

The Ewings intentionally rent out their properties for rents that are a bit less than market rate (5% to 10%), which they say helps with quickly renting them out and also keeping long-term tenants.

"Other landlords might think we are crazy, but it works for us," says Ann. "While we are a company and have to cover our expenses and generate enough money to invest in future renovations, we are also on a mission to improve communities."

And over the course of the last 20+ years, the Ewings have done just that.

"We rented [out] a one-bedroom property to an Army veteran who received a Section 8 voucher from the VA," says Ann. "We literally helped her move from a tent in the woods behind a fast-food restaurant into the first stable housing she had had in years."

Another example is an immigrant family that would not qualify for conventional bank financing to buy a home in the United States.

"Many years ago they rented from us for three years and always paid their rent on time and in full," says Ann. "They asked if they could purchase the house from us and we sold it to them, acting as the mortgage holder." Now, that family and their four children are very close to paying off their house.

The Ewings say they follow three principles in running their business.

First, treat everyone with respect and dignity. As they say, customer service is key to any business.

"Even if we don't have a property that would work for a particular person, we may be able to help someone else that they know," says Ann.

Second, they will not rent out a property that they would not live in themselves.

"While we may prefer a different number of bedrooms or a different layout, we will not rent [out] a property unless it is a clean, safe, decent place to live," says Ann.

Third, all of their renovations are done with an eye toward energy efficiency.

"We will invest extra money upfront to help people keep their utility bills low," the couple adds. "This is good for the tenants, it is good for us because happy tenants tend to renew their leases, and it is good for the environment. Win-win-win!"

The Ewings have also deliberately remained very hands-on throughout the process over the years.

"All of our properties are in Jackson, TN, or just beyond the city limits into Madison County," states Ann, explaining that she and Frank made a decision early on not to purchase a property more than a 15-minute drive from their home. "Managing property can be challenging enough when you are near it, and it gets exponentially more difficult the further away it is."

Though they recently turned management of a few properties over to a local property manager to free up some of their personal time for other pursuits, they are still managing several of their properties themselves and continue to look for ways to expand their mission.

"We are currently working on a duplex built in 1925 that we are bringing up to 2026 standards, and once this is complete, we may look for another property," says Ann.

After more than 20 years of turning "Housing Into Homes," the Ewings are now on a quest to teach other people how they can "do well by doing good" (their unofficial motto).

That was one reason they wrote their book—to give others the tools and a blueprint on how they can help others and help themselves at the same time by turning real estate investments into affordable housing.

"It is psychologically rewarding to turn a run-down property into a beautiful home," says Ann. "Making a difference in people's lives is an awesome bonus!"

#5625. Five9 buys contact center intelligence startup Level AI after posting narrow earnings beat

Contact center company Five9 Inc. flexed its acquisitive muscles today as it announced a $325 million all-cash deal to buy an artificial intelligence-native rival called Level AI as it posted its third-quarter financial results.

The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter, subject to customary closing conditions. Five9 is a leading player in the cloud contact center software industry, selling tools and services that enterprises use to manage their customer service interactions. Its web-based software spans traditional phone calls, video calls, emails, messaging, social media and other channels.

As for Level AI, it’s the developer of a contact center and customer experience intelligence platform that uses artificial intelligence to support human agents on calls and analyze, score and augment their interactions with the callers they serve. Its platform is designed to listen into customer service agent’s calls, so it can provide real-time guidance throughout and support workflow automation. The insights it generates can also be used to assist in agent coaching.

Level AI also develops autonomous AI agents that can automate some simpler customer inquiries and background operational tasks, freeing up human agents to focus on more complex customer issues. “Level AI’s AI applications help organizations improve agent performance, automate more customer interactions across voice and digital channels, and turn conversations into insights the whole organization can use,” Five9 said in a blog post announcing the deal. “Its applications are in production with enterprise customers today and handle more than 1 billion customer interactions a year.”

Five9 said it intends to continue offering Level AI’s applications as standalone tools for organizations that don’t want to shift their on-premises contact center operations to the cloud, also those who are using other cloud contact center platforms. However, it also plans to integrate the startup’s tools with its Genius CX Platform.

“As AI reshapes the customer experience landscape, we believe adding Level AI strengthens our competitive position, expands the customers we can serve, and deepens the AI talent behind our continuous innovation,” said Five9 Chief Executive Amit Mathradas.

Level AI founder and CEO Ashish Nagar said that by joining Five9, his company will be able to bring its applications and customer service-native AI models to thousands of new contact centers around the world, while allowing it to continue supporting its existing customers.

Investors don’t seem to have shared the CEOs’ enthusiasm for the deal, however, for Five9’s stock fell more than 23% in late trading after the deal was announced. That may be because of the cost of the acquisition. The $325 million cash outlay amounts to almost half of Five9’s current cash and marketable investments, which stood at $738 million at the end of the third quarter.

Five9’s results weren’t too bad. The company reported adjusted earnings of 82 cents per share on revenue of $323.3 million, surpassing Wall Street’s guidance of 80 cents per share in earnings and $318.3 million in sales. But it’s notable that the company’s full-year guidance excludes any contributions from the pending deal, and so its value hinges on Five9’s ability to rapidly integrate Level AI’s technology.

For the current quarter, Five9 said it’s expecting earnings of between 88 and 92 cents per share on sales of $328 million to $334 million. But that guidance was mixed. Wall Street is looking for significantly higher earnings of 99 cents per share and $330.7 million in revenue.

For the full year, Five9 said it’s looking for earnings of $3.17 to $3.21 per share on total sales of $1.27 billion. Wall Street wants to see higher earnings of $3.26 per share on similar revenue.

#5624. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5623. Home prices rise in 78% of metros while weekly demand sinks to a low

Prices climbed in 78 percent of metros in the third quarter, according to NAR, as Redfin data shows pending sales at the lowest level in its records.

Home prices rose in 78 percent of U.S. metro areas during the third quarter, while pending sales in the four weeks ending Oct. 25 fell to the lowest level in Redfin’s records.

The national median single-family existing-home price rose 1.7 percent year over year to $432,900, matching the second quarter’s revised annual growth rate, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday. Prices rose in 78 percent of the some 235 metros NAR tracks, down from 80 percent in the second quarter, and fell in 21 percent, up from 20 percent. Four percent of metros posted double-digit gains, down from 5 percent.

“Even with affordability challenges causing the housing market to stagnate, home prices continue to set record highs in most parts of the country,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Homeowners are the beneficiaries of the price gains. Over the past seven years, the average house has appreciated by $146,000.”

Redfin’s data for the four weeks ending Oct. 25 shows prices dipping. The median U.S. home-sale price fell 0.1 percent year over year to $389,601, according to Redfin, following a 0.2 percent decline the prior week. The two drops are the first in more than three years.

NAR and Redfin measure different things. NAR tracks quarterly sales of existing single-family homes, while Redfin’s figures cover homes listed or sold across more than 900 metros on a rolling four-week basis.

The Northeast posted the largest annual gain, and the West was the only region where prices fell, according to NAR.

Prices declined in many Florida markets over the past year, Yun said.

“This quarter, however, homes in nearly all Florida markets are showing price gains,” he said. “In a similar vein, price declines in other markets may also be brief if the local job market and economy are solid.”

Gulfport-Biloxi-Pascagoula, Mississippi, led large markets with an 11 percent price increase, followed by Rochester, New York (10.9 percent) and Jackson, Mississippi (10.1 percent). Grand Rapids-Wyoming, Michigan; Cleveland-Elyria, Ohio; and Fort Wayne, Indiana, were among the Midwest markets in the top 10.

“Many markets in the Midwest offer exceptional value with more affordable homes, making homeownership more attainable,” Yun said. “Meanwhile, the artificial intelligence technology boom continues to push Bay Area home prices higher, keeping the region the most expensive in the country.”

San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, California, remained the most expensive market at a median of $1.92 million, up 0.3 percent. Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine, California ($1.47 million) and San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, California ($1.35 million) followed. Nine of the 10 most expensive markets are in California or Hawaii.

The monthly mortgage payment on a typical existing single-family home with a 20 percent down payment was $2,251 in the third quarter, up $48 from the second quarter and $69 from a year earlier, according to NAR. Typical families spent an average of 24.1 percent of income on mortgage payments, up from 23.9 percent last quarter and down from 24.5 percent a year ago.

First-time buyers faced a monthly payment of $2,208 on a typical $368,000 starter home with 10 percent down. That payment took up 36.3 percent of income, up from 36 percent last quarter and down from 37 percent a year earlier.

Pending sales fell 1.8 percent from a week earlier and 15.9 percent year over year, declining in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metros for the third straight week, according to Redfin. Seattle (down 31.6 percent) and Atlanta (down 25.9 percent) posted the steepest annual drops.

Redfin’s median monthly mortgage payment, calculated at a 7.32 percent rate, reached $2,786, up 10.7 percent year over year and the second-highest level in its records. The weekly average rate is down from 7.4 percent a week earlier and near a three-year high.

New listings fell 0.6 percent from a week earlier to their lowest level since January. Total inventory rose 0.3 percent because pending sales fell faster than new listings, Redfin reported. The share of listings with price drops rose to 21.5 percent from 20.9 percent a year earlier.

Redfin reported hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they have had in more than a decade.

A First American analysis found that since 1991, rising mortgage rates have coincided with falling national home prices in some cases. In eight periods of sustained mortgage-rate increases since 1993, national home prices generally continued to appreciate, though the pace varied, First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming found.

During the rate run-up from December 2021 through October 2023, national prices rose an estimated 14 percent, according to the analysis. Affordability worsened at a steeper rate than prices, Fleming found. First American’s Real House Price Index, which adjusts prices for changes in income and mortgage rates, rose more than 70 percent over the same period.

Limited inventory can offset weaker demand when rates rise, Fleming wrote. Homeowners with mortgages below current rates may hold off on selling, and some sellers pull homes from the market rather than accept lower prices.

“Higher mortgage rates can put pressure on home prices, but the economy, household incomes and the number of homes for sale all play a role in what happens next,” Fleming wrote.

#5622. Ryan Serhant Reveals the Turning Point That Made Him a Real Estate Star—and How He Thinks Agents Can Cash In on AI

Before Ryan Serhant became a recognizable face in real estate, he was one of thousands of agents showing up to an open casting call—and declaring himself the best in the universe.

The opportunity would put him on “Million Dollar Listing” and turn him into what he described as a “walking billboard,” giving him a platform he was determined to make count.

Speaking at NAR NXT 2026 in New Orleans, Serhant reflected on that career-changing break, the relentless social media strategy that followed, and why he believes agents should now be looking to artificial intelligence to help build their businesses.

His message to agents navigating an uncertain market was straightforward: “Markets don’t dictate your income. They dictate your strategy.”

For Serhant, learning where to direct his energy was part of that process. He recalled spending too much time early in his career stressing about things he could not control, including what might happen in the months ahead.

Instead, he encouraged agents to focus on the work they can tackle now. The future will arrive regardless, and worrying about it does little to move a business forward.

"I try to plan ahead and I don't even—as an agent and a CEO— I'd be stressed about what is going to happen and one of the mistakes in the beginning of my career was stressing about what I can't control," he said, adding that agents should "attack" what they can control "without worrying about the future."

Branding himself a "futurist," he added, “At the end of the day, no one knows what they are doing."

Serhant acknowledged that his first few years were difficult and suggested that getting started as an agent is even harder today. His own breakthrough came after he attended an open casting call for “Million Dollar Listing” in 2010, joining roughly 3,000 real estate agents in Times Square.

He recalled not fully knowing what he would be doing there. But when asked why he had come, he delivered an answer that left little room for self-doubt: “I’m the greatest real estate agent in the universe.”

Serhant revealed the season was filmed with four people, but only three ultimately made the cut.

Once the show aired, he recognized that the exposure had given him an opportunity to distinguish himself—and he felt compelled to capitalize on it.

“Once the show came out, I became a walking billboard,” he said.

He also acknowledged the role timing played in his rise. He was finding his footing professionally as both cable television and social media offered opportunities to reach potential customers.

“I need to meet my customer where my customer is,” he said.

That approach led him to embrace Instagram in its early days, posting photographs of listings with himself in the images. He recalled posting every two to three hours, steadily building an audience that could become familiar with him before ever meeting him.

The goal was to establish a presence on people’s phones, creating recognition that could carry into an eventual conversation or business relationship.

Today, Serhant said, helping other agents succeed has become a source of excitement in its own right.

“It makes me tick. I enjoy it. I love it,” he said of teaching others.

Having encountered a wide range of challenges throughout his career, he described watching his agents win as the work that now gets him most excited.

He also emphasized his belief in investing in the future, describing Serhant’s mission as helping the world move forward.

For agents considering what that future looks like, artificial intelligence was a central part of his advice.

“The excitement within AI isn’t just language. It’s in creating work,” he said.

Serhant encouraged agents to identify administrative tasks that technology could reduce, freeing up time for the activities that depend on human connection and creativity.

“Humans should be doing only what humans do, which is meeting and creating,” he said.

He pointed to negotiation support and homeownership information as potential uses, while urging agents to think beyond individual tasks and consider how AI could help generate more business.

The measures that matter, he suggested, include increasing transactions per agent and improving gross profit. In that framing, the value of adopting AI lies in what it enables an agent to accomplish.

But he also shared an anecdote illustrating how the technology can influence a client’s decisions.

Serhant recalled a buyer pulling out of a $50 million deal after asking ChatGPT whether they were paying too much and receiving an affirmative answer.

The account underscored a challenge for agents: clients can now arrive with AI-generated conclusions that affect their willingness to move forward with a purchase.

His advice was to use the technology as support in their own work.

Across his reflections on television, social media, and AI, Serhant returned to the importance of approaching opportunities with a willingness to act.

“I learned that optimists are successful," he said.

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. #5621. How Kyle Whissel built eXp’s top real estate team

The San Diego-based CEO recruits up to 15 agents a month, has a dress code and gives his trainer authority to cut newcomers.

Kyle Whissel has a standing instruction for his “60-day” bootcamp trainers: they should be willing to cut people.

His team brings in 10 to 15 new agents a month, puts them through approximately 60 hours of training over two weeks, and gives the trainer a goal of removing two people from each class.

It’s a striking approach from the leader of eXp Realty’s highest-volume U.S. team in San Diego, California. Whissel is CEO of the Whissel Beer Group, formed in 2025 when his Whissel Realty Group merged with Daniel Beer’s Beer Home Team.

According to Whissel, the team made $875 million in sales volume across 1,042 transaction sides last year (it was the first team in San Diego to break 1,000). The median price in San Diego — which is where he likes to focus his attention  (“we love that median price,” he said) — is around $1 million, he told Inman.

They’ve done that by hiring — and retaining — the right people. “We’ll give people an opportunity to prove themselves … but we’ve grown far more by cutting people than simply by hiring more people,” Whissel told Inman‘s Taylor Anderson during an interview at eXpcon in Salt Lake City earlier this month.

The company’s saying: “Expectations without enforcement are simply suggestions.”

Whissel’s recruiting process starts with a conventional, short interview, but he views the company’s two-week training period as a far better measure of whether someone belongs on the team.

Spending 60 hours in training gives leadership a chance to observe how that person behaves, learns and responds to expectations. Role-playing and scripting exercises also reveal whether new agents have the communication skills needed to work with clients.

The process continues after training, too. New agents are assigned mentors, and Whissel said those mentors are empowered to recommend removing someone who fails to meet team standards.

“If you’re going to be disrespectful to our team, I’ll be damned if I’m going to give you a client because you’re probably going to be disrespectful to them too,” he said.

Whissel also has activity and production expectations for agents already on the team. They include participating in role-playing sessions and attending meetings, along with meeting production targets.

Whissel’s hiring philosophy reaches back to his own first job, scooping popcorn at a movie theater, where he would compete with others to see who could serve the most customers. He looks for that same competitiveness in prospective agents, even if their previous accomplishments have little to do with real estate.

An applicant who participated in a college sorority, for example, might be asked whether they held a leadership position. Whissel said he wants to understand whether someone has a history of taking initiative.

In August 2025, Inman reported the merger of Whissel Realty Group and Beer Home Team, two of eXp’s highest-producing organizations. The combined company launched with approximately 160 agents and more than 60 staff members across five offices.

He said the first six months involved understanding the two organizations’ systems and getting them aligned. Whissel now believes it could take 18 months to fully integrate the companies.

“We’re going to be almost flat year-over-year,” he said, referring to the team’s expected 2026 performance, “but we’re setting up for a really, really big 2027,” he said. “You’ve gotta take a step back to take two steps forward.”

He remains optimistic about 2027, when he expects the operational investments to begin contributing to stronger growth.

Agents need to understand assumable mortgages, he said. “If you are working with a seller … and you’re not asking questions to figure out ‘does this seller have an assumable mortgage?’ (If it’s FHA, VA or USDA, those are assumable), I’m gonna beat you, because I am asking those questions.”

To find out whether a mortgage is assumable, agents simply need to get the closing disclosure from the seller. “It’s simple,” he said.
