#5533. 8 ways to stay warm and cut your heating bill this winter, according to AAA

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Sealing drafts, using sunlight, lowering the thermostat, and maintaining your heater can trim winter energy use, even for renters.

Cold weather has a way of turning home comfort into a money question. Hot drinks come out, holiday decorations go up, and the thermostat starts getting a lot more attention. Then the utility statement lands. The U.S. Department of Energy reports that heating can swallow nearly a third of a household's utility bill. A cost of that size returns every winter. Small decisions about how a home holds its temperature, and how the people inside stay cozy, can shift a meaningful slice of that spending.

Prices in 2021 sharpened the squeeze. The New York Times reported that natural gas went for double its 2020 level that year, with heating oil and propane climbing as well. The U.S. Energy Information Administration projected at the time that a somewhat colder-than-normal winter could push bills up 94 percent for propane users, 50 percent for natural gas customers, and 15 percent for those with electric heat. The agency was describing a possible winter, yet its numbers showed how far a cold snap could stretch a budget tied to one fuel. The most effective structural defenses carry a steep price of their own. Insulation and windows with two or three panes keep warmth inside better than any other strategy, but retrofitting an existing building with them can prove expensive. Many renters cannot make major changes to the places they lease.

Via, the magazine of AAA Mountain West Group, published a tip sheet by Mandy Ferreira on Nov. 22, 2021, laying out eight tasks and habits for owners and tenants alike. The piece compiles advice. It reports no survey, test, or original analysis of its own. Its figures come from outside authorities it names, among them the U.S. Department of Energy, the U.S. Energy Information Administration, The New York Times, and Pacific Gas and Electric. A few estimates appear without any named source. Readers should treat its dollar figures and forecasts as a 2021 snapshot. The list below covers every tip in the magazine's lineup, in sequence, and each one stays within reach of anyone who can't take on a renovation.

Light or moving air at the spot where an exterior door meets its jamb signals a need for new weatherstripping, and a door without any stripping deserves its first set. An evening spent next to a leaky window teaches how much cold can push through cracks and seams that seem too narrow to matter. Such openings act as stealthy thieves of heat, and strips of weatherstripping and beads of caulk shut them down.

Air infiltration, the movement of outside air in and out through gaps in a building's shell, drives up heating and cooling bills and leaves occupants less comfortable. Ill-fitting doors and windows, the line where a house sits on its foundation, and the holes around pipes and wiring that pierce the walls all give that air an easy path. A leak at any joint, including where brick or wood siding meets the foundation or walls, admits moisture that can warp wood and contribute to mold.

Daylight around a door or window frame offers one clue to a draft, and a homeowner can shake windows and doors to see whether they shift or run a hand along caulk lines to feel a current. Incense smoke or a damp hand can reveal the flow, and a basic building pressurization test makes leaks easier to find. A lamp outside a closed door exposes gaps in jamb stripping by shining through wherever the door fails to meet its stop.

Weatherstripping earns a place beyond entry doors, sealing the hatch to an attic or crawlspace. Run caulk along baseboards and the edges of window frames, and inspect the stripping on any window that opens, swapping it out once it wears thin. Caulk belongs at the joint between a window frame and the outer wall, but it should stay out of the channel between sash and jamb, where it would lock the window shut. Weatherstripping handles that space. The material comes in strips built to stop drafts around the moving parts of doors and windows while those parts sit closed. Vinyl or metal V-strip demands cutting tools and some skill to install, which may put it beyond some do-it-yourselfers.

Outlets and light switches set in uninsulated walls can let cold air through, and foam gaskets seal those openings. Most of these checks rely on sight or touch, letting a household pinpoint its leaks before buying any materials.

About three-quarters of the sunlight striking a double-paned window passes through the glass and becomes heat inside the room. The pane works as a small heater that never sends a bill. Any household with sun-facing double-paned windows owns a source of warmth it does not have to buy.

Opening curtains and blinds on windows that catch direct sun during the day captures that energy at no cost. A closed blind halts the light short of the room, and the warmth the light would have carried never arrives. Leaving coverings shut through a bright afternoon means paying the furnace to replace heat the sun offered for nothing. The habit requires no tools, no purchase, and no landlord's approval. Tenants who cannot alter the glass itself can put it to work.

Orientation determines how much a window can contribute. Green Building Advisor reports that in data for Providence, R.I., south-facing windows delivered more daylight and solar heat than windows facing any other direction between September and April. The same figures showed a single south-facing window outgaining three windows facing north, east, and west combined from November through February. Rooms on the south side of a home deserve the first attention when the blinds go up each morning. A home whose main windows face north, east, or west will collect a smaller share of this free warmth. Its occupants will get more mileage from the other tips in this lineup.

Climate sets a second boundary. Anchorage, Alaska, stood alone in the outlet's January comparison of cities as the place where heat escaping through south-facing glass exceeded the solar gain. Every other city on the list came out ahead, with sunshine through south windows outweighing what the panes lost. Outside that one northern outlier, the data give households in those cities a reason to raise south-facing blinds on January days.

Tight-fitting cellular shades, also called honeycomb shades, cut the heat a window loses by at least 40 percent, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. The agency equates that reduction at the glass with about 10 percent less energy spent on heating. The two numbers describe different scales. The larger one covers a single window, while the smaller one spans a home's entire heating load. The gap between them suggests windows account for only part of the warmth a house loses.

Pleated, creased fabric gives these shades their structure. The folds form pockets shaped something like hexagons, and the whole shade moves up and down to open and close. Each shade carries two layers of pleating, according to tucson.com. One pocket of air sits inside the shade itself, and a second forms in the space between the shade and the window glass. Trapped air in both places pays off most in colder climates.

Heavy drapes and insulated curtains make strong alternatives to cellular shades for keeping a room warm after dark. Shutters offer another approach. Their frame mounts to the wall around a window, and the gap left between the glass and the room serves as a layer of insulation. The air space protects less than the insulation inside walls. Every option here places a barrier between the room and the cold panes, yet the federal number covers snug cellular shades alone, leaving drapes, curtains, and shutters without a measured payoff.

Adding a layer before touching the thermostat puts heat where a person feels it. The advice flips the usual winter reflex and asks people to take care of their bodies before they turn to the air around them. The wardrobe portion starts at the floor with cozy socks and slippers, then climbs to sweaters and a blanket. Every item on that list is ordinary clothing or bedding, and none of it draws power.

A toasty drink or a hot meal heats a person from the inside out. Daily habits, such as a morning mug or an evening dinner, become part of the household's defense against the cold. The kettle and stove take over a small share of the furnace's work.

Electric blankets and reusable heat packs bring comfort in short order and use minimal energy. CHOICE home heating expert Chris Barnes said heated throws are energy efficient and use less electricity than a portable heater or air conditioner. A plug-in throw sits between a sweater and the furnace. It supplies active warmth to one person and leaves the rest of the house out of the arrangement. A reusable pack works through many rounds, sparing the buyer a repeat purchase.

Renters can follow every step here. None calls for a tool, a contractor, a landlord's sign-off, or a single change to the building itself. The underlying logic comes down to scale. A blanket covers one body, while a central system heats every room it serves, occupied or empty. The habits hold up no matter which fuel feeds the furnace, whether propane, natural gas, or electricity. The article's subtitle pitches its tips as a way to shrink both a carbon footprint and a utility bill. Clothing, food, and heat packs serve both goals, letting a household dial back the heat without feeling the chill.

Dropping the thermostat 7 to 10 degrees at night or during work hours can shave up to 10% off heating costs. Night and the workday cover the stretches when a household sleeps under the covers or leaves the house empty. Few people notice a cooler room from under a comforter or from a desk across town.

Waking hours at home call for 68 degrees or lower. The two targets add up to a daily rhythm. A modest temperature holds while people move around the house, and a deeper dip follows once they go to bed or head out the door.

Pacific Gas and Electric credits a programmable thermostat, which keeps temperatures in line with a household's schedule, with savings of up to $180 a year. These devices switch heating or air conditioning on at preset times, according to Energy.gov. A schedule takes memory out of the equation. The overnight and workday drops depend on someone remembering to make them twice a day, and a programmed routine handles both without a reminder.

Smart thermostats push control past the front door, letting owners change the temperature from wherever they happen to be. A forgotten adjustment on the way out no longer commits a household to warming empty rooms all day.

Heat pump owners may need to skip the daily dips. Energy.gov reports that programmable thermostats used to be a poor fit for heat pumps, though a few manufacturers now build models for those systems that make a setback cost effective. A heat pump guide on Energy.gov tells owners of air-source units to hold the thermostat steady for the best efficiency. Switching one off in an empty home can trigger wasteful operation once the system restarts. The guide reserves setbacks for absences longer than a day.

A heat pump owner who wants nightly savings should confirm that the thermostat's maker designed it for that equipment, and otherwise save deeper setbacks for trips that last more than a day.

A washing machine can devote as much as 90% of the energy in a typical cycle to heating water, which hands the temperature dial outsized control over what each load costs. Everything else the machine does during a wash splits the remainder. Anyone hoping to shave the laundry room's share of a winter utility bill can start with a single knob.

Switching from hot to warm halves the energy a load requires. Turning the dial to cold cuts consumption by more than 50%. Each step down targets the same expense, the heating of the water, so the savings come out of the largest slice of the cycle's demand. Every cold load repeats the reduction, and the total grows with each wash through the heating season.

Air drying pushes the gains past the washer. An indoor rack lets clothes dry without the machine whenever space allows, and an outdoor line works on days free of rain and freezing temperatures. In the coldest stretch of winter, that limit steers drying toward the indoor rack. Skipping the dryer conserves power and spares fabric, which helps garments last longer.

A longer cycle at lower heat draws less energy than a hot, fast run, even though the clothes take more time to finish. Households that keep the dryer in their routine can trade time for a smaller energy draw.

The Department of Energy recommends that anyone shopping for a new dryer choose a model with a moisture sensor. The sensor switches the machine off once the clothes reach dryness, which keeps the drum from tumbling a finished load. The agency adds that the feature trims energy use and limits the wear that over-drying inflicts on clothing.

Across washer and dryer, the same pattern holds. Less heat shrinks spending at every stage of the laundry routine, from the wash to the final tumble.

LED bulbs draw more than 75 percent less energy than incandescent bulbs, and each one shines 25 times longer before it burns out. Every swap leaves a fixture pulling less than a quarter of the electricity it once used. The savings grow with use, and a lamp that burns for hours each evening returns the most. The change demands no new habits once the bulb sits in the socket. A household flips the same switches as before and collects the reward.

Longevity reshapes the math of keeping a room lit. One LED can serve as long as 25 incandescents installed one after another. A home that switches buys fewer replacements and spends less time swapping dead bulbs. Its power bill and its shopping list shrink together. The bulbs leave the heating system untouched, yet they pare down the electric portion of the same utility statement. The benefit also outlasts the cold months. A thermostat setback pays off while the furnace runs, whereas an efficient bulb keeps saving through spring and summer.

Holiday strings carry the advantage into decorating season. LED string lights run cooler than incandescent strands and can keep glowing for decades. As many as 25 strands can draw from a single socket, enough to power a sprawling display from one outlet. A set bought once can return each winter for years.

Timers and smart plugs attack waste from the other direction. They switch festive lighting on once darkness falls and shut it off at bedtime. Nobody has to remember to unplug the decorations, and no power flows to lights shining over a sleeping house. The devices impose on holiday lights the same schedule-driven discipline a programmable thermostat brings to heating.

Efficient bulbs lower the price of every lit hour, and a timer erases the hours nobody sees. Together they squeeze the lighting bill from both ends.

A furnace air filter needs cleaning or replacing once a month through the winter, or on the schedule its manufacturer recommends. The chore opens a short upkeep routine that helps a heating system waste less energy. Each step targets a different spot where a home's heat can stall or slip away.

Baseboard heaters, radiators, and warm-air registers work best when they stay clean and free of obstructions. A sofa pushed flush against a baseboard unit or a curtain draped over a register stands between the room and the output the system produces. Sliding furniture a few inches and tying back drapes cost nothing.

An open fireplace damper on a night without a fire leaves a direct opening between the living room and the outdoors. Closing the damper whenever the fireplace sits idle shuts off that route. A chimney the household no longer uses needs its flue sealed for good.

Any ductwork within reach needs solid insulation and airtight seals. The ducts carry warm air from the furnace to each room, and gaps or bare runs along the way spend that heat before it arrives.

A heat pump can cut the electricity a home uses for heating by up to 50%, and the same equipment handles cooling in summer. In cold months, a heat pump moves warmth indoors from the outside air, and in warm months it sends indoor warmth outside. Homes without ductwork can use an air-source model in its ductless form, known as a mini-split.

A ductless mini-split pairs an outdoor unit with one or more head units mounted on an interior wall or ceiling. The outdoor unit pulls heat from the air despite low temperatures, and refrigerant carries that heat straight to the indoor heads. Four of the five steps here tune equipment a home has in place, and the heat pump alone calls for buying a new system.

#5532. Filing: Amazon’s previously announced layoffs include 95 jobs in Washington state

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 6:11 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 7:26 am

A notice made public Tuesday evening, disclosing about 95 Amazon job cuts in Washington state, is part of the company’s previously reported layoffs in its retail business, not a new round of reductions, a spokesperson confirmed.

The filing lists software engineers, product managers and program managers among the affected employees. Most are based in Amazon’s Seattle offices, but others work in Bellevue and Redmond, at warehouses in Sumner and Pasco, or remotely.

Reuters reported in early October that Amazon was laying off fewer than 1,000 corporate employees, mainly in its Stores unit, which runs the company’s e-commerce business. Amazon confirmed to GeekWire at the time that “hundreds” of Stores employees were affected. The notice covers only employees based in Washington state.

“We’ve adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure will better enable us to deliver on our priorities,” Amazon said in a statement at the time.

Most affected employees were notified in October, including 43 on or about Oct. 7, when the Stores cuts were first reported. Others received notice in September or as early as July 3, according to the filing.

The federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act requires large employers to give workers and the government advance notice of mass layoffs. Washington’s version of the WARN Act generally requires 60 days’ notice when a covered employer eliminates 50 or more jobs within 30 days across its Washington operations, excluding part-time employees.

Amazon has made a series of smaller filings under the state law in the past year, including notices covering 121 jobs in August, 57 tech jobs earlier in the summer and 84 jobs last December.

The latest notice covers employees at 17 Amazon offices and warehouses in Seattle, Bellevue, Redmond, Sumner and Pasco, plus 15 remote workers in the state.

The list also includes risk managers, several directors and other senior employees. Employees who land other jobs inside Amazon before their separation dates won’t be laid off, the notice says.

The Stores cuts were much smaller than Amazon’s major corporate cutbacks since last fall. The company eliminated about 14,000 corporate roles globally in October 2025, including 2,303 in Washington, followed by another round in January that included 2,198 Washington employees.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5531. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.

#5530. A new group of senators from both parties will vote on how to save Social Security. Here’s what they’ve said about it

Democrats rode a blue wave of Senate pickups on Tuesday, flipping seven seats in red states and winning control of the chamber, while Republicans will also see some fresh faces. Together, the 17 newcomers from both parties will join the next Congress in taking on one of Washington’s most-dodged problems: how to keep Social Security paying full benefits.

The program’s trust fund is projected to run dry in late 2032. After that, payroll tax revenue would cover only about 78% of scheduled benefits—forcing an automatic cut of roughly 22% unless Congress acts.

Senators elected to full terms this week serve until January 2033, so the deadline falls on their watch. And because Social Security can’t be changed through budget reconciliation, a fix will likely need 60 votes and support from both parties.

Nearly all the newcomers addressed Social Security during their campaigns. As Fortune previously reported, the issue isn’t quite the third rail it used to be, but “protecting” the program can mean very different things.

Here’s what each incoming senator has actually said they would do.

Juliana Stratton, D-Illinois — Stratton said she would eliminate the cap on wages subject to the payroll tax, according to The Times Weekly. Social Security payroll taxes now apply only to the first $184,500 of a worker’s yearly earnings. Eliminating that cap starting in 2027, without increasing benefits for the additional earnings taxed, would close an estimated 58% of Social Security’s projected 75-year funding shortfall, according to the Social Security Administration’s actuaries.

Josh Turek, D-Iowa — Turek said he would lift the $184,500 cap and opposes raising the age for full benefits.

Adam Hamilton, D-Kansas — Hamilton would raise the earnings cap rather than eliminate it, arguing that someone earning $1 million shouldn’t pay the same Social Security tax as someone earning $184,500. He didn’t take a firm position on the retirement age.

Andy Barr, R-Kentucky — Barr opposed changes for people already retired and called for bipartisan reforms for younger generations. He didn’t name specific tax or benefit changes but said reforms should encourage more private and employer-sponsored retirement savings.

Troy Jackson, D-Maine — In a September Bangor Daily News op-ed, Jackson called for scrapping the payroll tax cap and increasing benefits, while ruling out privatization and raising the retirement age.

Abdul El-Sayed, D-Michigan — In his final debate, El-Sayed said the payroll tax cap should be removed and that Social Security benefits shouldn’t be taxed.

Eliminating taxes on benefits without replacing revenue would cost Social Security about $1 trillion over 10 years, plus an additional $700 billion for Medicare, according to a July analysis published by the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.

Peggy Flanagan, D-Minnesota — Flanagan backs Sen. Bernie Sanders’ Social Security Expansion Act, Bloomberg Government reported. The bill would apply payroll taxes to wages above $250,000, eventually eliminate the cap, and raise benefits. Her campaign site also supports eliminating taxes on benefits.

Kurt Alme, R-Montana — Alme says savings from cutting waste, fraud, and abuse elsewhere in government should go toward Social Security. In an October debate, he pointed to his experience as Montana’s budget director but didn’t propose changes to the cap or the benefit formula.

Chris Pappas, D-New Hampshire — Pappas opposes raising the retirement age, cutting benefits, and privatization. His campaign highlighted his cosponsorship of the Social Security Fairness Act, the 2025 law that boosted benefits for public workers with outside pensions.

Roy Cooper, D-North Carolina — Cooper made the 2032 deadline a staple of his stump speech. He opposes benefit cuts and says wealthy Americans should contribute more to the program but hasn’t specified how.

Annie Andrews, D-South Carolina — Andrews supports eliminating taxes on Social Security benefits but hasn’t laid out a plan to close the funding gap yet.

James Talarico, D-Texas — Talarico wants to eliminate the payroll tax cap for people earning over $400,000, Texas Public Radio reported.

Barry Moore, R-Alabama — Moore’s Senate campaign website backed cutting taxes on Social Security benefits. He was also an original cosponsor of the Senior Citizens Tax Elimination Act, introduced in February 2025. The bill would remove Social Security benefits from federal taxable income and transfer general funds to replace the revenue the trust funds would lose.

Harriet Hageman, R-Wyoming — Asked how to prevent Social Security cuts during an August 2026 primary debate, Hageman said growing the economy, creating jobs, and getting more people into the workforce would help shore up the program. Like Moore, Hageman was an original cosponsor of the 2025 bill to end federal income taxes on benefits.

#5529. Starfish Space loses contact with its Otter spacecraft, ending satellite inspection mission

by Alan Boyle on Nov 3, 2026 at 10:50 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 11:10 pm

Starfish Space says it can no longer receive data from its first full-scale Otter space vehicle, bringing a $15 million NASA mission to inspect inoperable satellites to a premature end.

In a LinkedIn post, the Tukwila, Wash.-based startup said its Otter 24C spacecraft was not able to complete all the objectives for the mission, known as Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability (SSPICY). “Starfish and NASA are exploring opportunities to fulfill mission objectives through other Starfish missions,” the company said.

The Otter spacecraft was sent into low Earth orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on Oct. 1. “Following a successful launch and deployment, Starfish established two-way contact with the spacecraft and successfully commanded Otter 24C, downlinking significant telemetry during early operations,” Starfish said.

However, the mission team lost contact with the oven-sized spacecraft during the commissioning process. “An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications,” the company said.

Starfish, NASA and Astro Digital determined that the spacecraft was unrecoverable.

In today’s update, Starfish said it is working closely with Astro Digital to fix the fault protection system and update testing procedures for future Otters.

“Developing new capabilities in space requires taking on difficult challenges, learning quickly and applying those lessons to what comes next,” Starfish said. “The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit.”

Greg Stover, director of the Advanced Research and Technology Division at NASA Headquarters, said in a news release that “commercial capabilities like Starfish’s are critical for a competitive U.S. space economy and strong American leadership in low Earth orbit.”

“Technology demonstrations allow us to quickly test new systems, learn from their performance, and iterate so that we are pushing the boundaries of what’s possible with every mission,” Stover said. “NASA will continue taking on bold challenges in close collaboration with our industry partners.”

Several other Otter missions remain on tap — including a satellite disposal job for the Pentagon’s Space Development Agency, two commercial satellite servicing missions in geostationary Earth orbit, and two servicing missions for the U.S. Space Force.

Starfish Space is also continuing to test an Otter Pup prototype that was launched into orbit last year. Last week, it posted a video to LinkedIn showing a close approach to a target satellite known as ElaraSat. The company says it is preparing for a docking attempt “and a chance to make history.”

#5528. Why Entrepreneurs Need to Stop Carrying Everything to Keep Their Business Growing

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Entrepreneurs are celebrated for how much responsibility they can handle. But as businesses grow, carrying everything can become the very thing holding them back.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Entrepreneurs are often praised for their ability to carry enormous responsibility. They build companies, manage employees, serve customers, make payroll and navigate uncertainty, sometimes all before lunch.

In the beginning, carrying everything can feel necessary. You become the salesperson, marketer, accountant and customer service department because there’s nobody else to do it.

But something changes as the business grows. The responsibilities multiply, and the habits that helped you survive the startup phase can become obstacles to sustainable success.

You may have built a thriving business while becoming exhausted, disconnected from your family or unable to imagine the company functioning without you.

The problem isn’t necessarily that you’re carrying too much. It’s that you haven’t reconsidered what you’re carrying, why you’re carrying it and whether it’s still yours to carry.

That’s the thinking behind a framework I call The Five Carries.

Entrepreneurial ambition can make overextension feel like commitment. Yet research suggests that passion alone doesn’t protect founders from exhaustion.

A study discussed in Harvard Business Review examined how entrepreneurial passion, work characteristics and beliefs about success relate to burnout. Its findings challenge the assumption that loving your business automatically makes relentless work sustainable.

The pressure extends beyond founders. Gallup’s State of the Global Workplace 2026 report found that global manager engagement declined from 31% in 2022 to 22% in 2025. Managers, like entrepreneurs, frequently navigate competing expectations without sufficient capacity to meet them.

The lesson isn’t that responsibility should be avoided. It’s that responsibility must be managed intentionally.

The Five Carries framework organizes those responsibilities into five directions.

Entrepreneurs may not have traditional bosses, but they still answer to investors, lenders, boards, customers and their own ambitions.

Carry Up involves managing those expectations without allowing them to dictate every decision.

Consider a founder who promises aggressive expansion to investors while privately recognizing that the team lacks the resources to deliver. Carrying up effectively means communicating reality, negotiating priorities and setting responsible expectations rather than making commitments the business cannot sustain.

Ask yourself: Whose expectations am I carrying, and have I agreed to more than I can responsibly deliver?

Leadership sometimes requires the courage to disappoint someone today to protect the business tomorrow.

Employees depend on business owners for direction, resources, opportunities and a working environment where they can succeed.

But carrying down doesn’t mean absorbing everyone’s problems.

A founder who personally resolves every employee challenge may feel indispensable while unintentionally preventing the team from developing independence.

Effective leadership involves providing clarity, coaching and accountability so others become increasingly capable.

Instead of asking, “How can I solve this for my team?” consider asking, “How can I help my team become capable of solving this without me?”

The objective isn’t to become less supportive. It’s to make support developmental rather than dependency-producing.

Entrepreneurship is rarely an individual achievement, even when one person’s name appears on the company.

Business partners, spouses, colleagues, suppliers and professional peers often carry consequences of entrepreneurial decisions.

Yet these relationships can receive whatever attention remains after urgent business demands.

The American Psychological Association’s 2024 Work in America survey found that 43% of workers reported typically feeling tense or stressed during the workday, rising to 61% among those experiencing lower psychological safety.

Although those findings aren’t specific to entrepreneurs, they illustrate why healthy working relationships deserve deliberate attention.

Carrying across means collaborating rather than controlling, communicating rather than assuming and recognizing that your success affects people who don’t report to you.

Ask yourself: Which important relationship is receiving the leftovers of my time, energy and attention?

Entrepreneurs can become so consumed with immediate demands that they neglect the future they’re supposedly building.

Carry Forward involves preparing for what comes next: succession, organizational resilience, financial security, leadership development and the legacy of the business.

Imagine two founders operating similarly profitable companies.

One remains involved in every significant decision. The other invests in systems, develops successors and builds a leadership team capable of operating independently.

Both may be successful today, but only one is deliberately reducing the company’s dependence on its founder.

Carrying forward requires moving beyond the question, “What does my business need from me today?”

It asks, “What must I build today, so the business and the people connected to it can thrive tomorrow?”

This may be the most overlooked responsibility of entrepreneurship.

Carry Within concerns the physical, mental and emotional capacity required to sustain everything else.

A founder can become so identified with the business that personal well-being feels secondary to professional achievement.

Sleep becomes negotiable. Exercise gets postponed. Family time becomes conditional. Recovery feels like something to earn after the next milestone.

But your business cannot continually draw from capacity you never replenish.

Carrying within isn’t about avoiding hard work. It’s about recognizing that the entrepreneur is part of the enterprise’s long-term sustainability.

If your business succeeds only while your health, relationships and sense of purpose deteriorate, it’s worth questioning what success actually means.

The Five Carries aren’t five additional responsibilities to pile onto an already crowded calendar. They’re five lenses for evaluating the responsibilities you already have.

Start with a simple exercise. Write down your biggest current obligations and identify which carry each belongs to. Then ask three questions:

What am I carrying? What am I going to carry? What am I finally ready to stop carrying?

You may discover that some responsibilities require greater attention, others need to be delegated and a few should never have remained yours in the first place.

Entrepreneurship will always involve responsibility. The goal isn’t to build a life without weight.

It’s to develop the judgment to carry what matters, share what shouldn’t be carried alone and release what no longer serves the future you’re building.

Because the ultimate measure of entrepreneurial success shouldn’t simply be how much you’ve managed to carry.

It should be what you’ve built, who you’ve helped and whether you still have the human capacity to enjoy it.

Entrepreneurs are often praised for their ability to carry enormous responsibility. They build companies, manage employees, serve customers, make payroll and navigate uncertainty, sometimes all before lunch.

In the beginning, carrying everything can feel necessary. You become the salesperson, marketer, accountant and customer service department because there’s nobody else to do it.

But something changes as the business grows. The responsibilities multiply, and the habits that helped you survive the startup phase can become obstacles to sustainable success.

#5527. ‘Like being hit between the eyes with a sledgehammer’: Meet the one town in America that defied election trends and voted in favor of data centers

In a midterm election punctuated by America’s overwhelming distaste for data centers, one small town in North Dakota has bucked the trend.

Of the 45 ballot measures on data centers this past election, only one went the pro-data center way, according to data from Redbud Consulting. That initiative belonged to Harwood, a North Dakota town 10 miles from Fargo and home to about 940 people, which overwhelmingly voted against a ballot measure that would place limitations on large-scale industrial developments such as data centers. About 75% (325) of the 430 votes cast on Tuesday opposed the measure.

Data centers were a major flashpoint of the midterm elections. With a new wave of moratoriums and restrictions, AI companies like OpenAI are scrambling to rebrand the buildout and market construction alongside promises of perks and community benefits to woo both local governments and residents.

The Harwood initiative proposed an amendment to the town’s Home Rule Charter that would impose requirements limiting how the city evaluates, approves, and administers development or building projects, such as requiring independent reviews and holding public hearings for industrial projects.

The measure was introduced following the ground-breaking of a 160-acre data center in Harwood, which Applied Digital Corp. was overseeing with Oracle as the end-user. The project was scheduled to be fully operational next year, and could possibly expand to 900 acres.

Michael Swartz, a senior software developer who’s lived in Harwood for nearly 20 years, said the town’s relationship with data centers perhaps isn’t as cut-and-dry as the election results suggest.

“Long term, there’s some really serious implications that I don’t think have been fully fleshed-out, or vetted, or even are getting talked about, at the scale that I think they need to be addressed,” Swartz told Fortune.

As the champion behind the ballot measure and the year-long fight against campus’s continued construction, Swartz believes the local data center expansion has the potential to harm the area, and that efforts to push the initiative were hampered by local authorities.

Harwood residents only learned about the data center construction about three weeks before construction for the data center began in Sept. 2025, according to Swartz. At the time, the Fargo Forum reported that then-Fargo Mayor Tim Mahoney and Harwood Mayor Blake Hankey both signed nondisclosure agreements with Applied Digital Corp. in July.

“When all of this came about, it was like being hit between the eyes with a sledgehammer,” Swartz’s wife Amanda told Fortune. “People deserve a say in projects of this scope.”

Nick Phillips, the executive vice president of external affairs at Applied Digital Corp., told Fortune the developer chose Harwood for its cooler climate and access to energy, as well as its “pro-business landscape and the ability to have a positive impact on the community, from job creation to economic benefits.”

“While our projects may seem fast to get going, they also involve an incredibly large amount of community conversations through both legally required as well as company-led events,” Phillips said in a statement. “We work very hard to provide a large amount of opportunities to learn about our potential projects before they are built including through town halls, one-on-one meetings, public forums, well above and beyond the public meeting requirements that exist.”

Swartz had concerns about the project, in particular, the levels of noise pollution associated with data centers, given the location of an elementary school within a mile or so of the campus. After a city council meeting—in which Swartz claims he wasn’t allowed to speak—he got in touch with other residents, with whom he formed the grassroots advocacy group Voices of Harwood and by January, had drafted a Home Rule Charter amendment, what they saw as a stronger measure than an ordinance, which can be changed by city council members. In August this year, the petition to get the measure on the ballot received 91 signatures, more than twice the mandatory 40, in just three days, Swartz said.

Then came the challenges. Swartz said in September, the Fargo Moorhead West Fargo Chamber of Commerce began disseminating anti-measure materials following Swartz’s distribution of a mailer that he paid for himself. Some of the materials, viewed by Fortune, claimed the passage of the measure would cost taxpayers an additional $300,000 to $544,000, and increase annual taxes due to lost projects by thousands of dollars.

Cale Dunwoody, vice president for public policy for the Fargo Moorhead West Fargo Chamber of Commerce, told Fortune in a statement that the body “worked closely with Harwood residents and businesses to provide voters with accurate information about the proposed amendment to the city’s home rule charter.”

Town officials, including Mayor Hankey, publicly opposed the measure, arguing the amendment would place an additional administrative burden on the town and set a precedent of requiring public votes for every town issue. Other officials like City Councilman Chris Higgins feared the measure would cause Applied Digital Corp. to de-annex the project, triggering a loss of tax benefits. Hankey said the data center would bring in $1.65 million in taxes by 2028. A North Dakota tax incentive would give Applied Digital Corp. a break from the state’s 5% sales tax on computers, cooling systems, and servers.

Swartz was also troubled by the language of the measure which eventually made it to the ballot, which he said differed significantly from what Voices of Harwood presented to the election committee, making it harder for voters to understand what the initiative was about.

“Had I not been involved with it, and had I not done my due diligence as a voter and read what Measure 2 was about, and I only was basing my decision on that summary, there’s no way I would have voted yes,” Swartz said.

A representative for Harwood City Council forwarded Fortune’s inquiry to the Mayor’s office. Hankey did not respond to Fortune’s requests for comment.

While Swartz was frustrated by how officials and stakeholders worked to oppose the measure, he attributed the failure to the same reason why many other data centers have faced roadblocks, and why Democrats saw an overwhelming victory on election night: affordability.

Pew Research Center found half of Americans said data centers would have a negative impact on their energy costs, but the prospect of losing out on tax benefits appeared to have been more salient to the small North Dakota town.

“We live in a climate right now where money is tight. Pocketbooks are getting squeezed by things that are way outside of our control,” Swartz said. “There’s people out there that are probably living paycheck-to-paycheck. They can’t afford to have more special assessments levied out on that monthly house payment. That would break them. I think that was a determining factor.”

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

#5526. Rover hires Textio co-founder Jensen Harris and former Amazon exec Vik Rajagopal

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:07 am

Seattle-based pet care marketplace Rover is adding two executives to its leadership team: former Motus CFO Vik Rajagopal as chief financial officer and Textio co-founder Jensen Harris as president of marketplace, product and technology.

Rajagopal succeeds Charlie Wickers, who served as Rover’s CFO from 2022 to 2025. Harris succeeds Brent Turner, who was Rover’s president and chief operating officer before he was named CEO last year.

Rajagopal spent nearly a decade at Amazon, starting in 2011 as a finance lead for Amazon Global Selling, the program that helps sellers reach customers in other countries. He later became a general manager in Amazon’s retail business, running the U.S. shoes and luggage stores and the home store, as well as Amazon’s U.S. Vendor Success Program.

He left Amazon in late 2020 to become CFO of Logos, a maker of Bible study software backed by private equity firm Cove Hill Partners. He was promoted to CEO about a year later, replacing the company’s founder, and led Logos until April 2024. He was most recently CFO at Motus, which makes software that companies use to manage and reimburse employees who drive for work.

Earlier in his career, Rajagopal was an investment banker at Wells Fargo Securities and worked in corporate development at Symantec. He holds a bachelor’s degree from Yale and an MBA from Northwestern’s Kellogg School of Management.

“Rover is a Seattle company that was built the right way from day one — solving a real customer pain point with a strong product, solid economics, and a culture that is poised for long-term success,” Rajagopal said in a news release on Wednesday.

Harris co-founded Seattle-based Textio in 2014 with Kieran Snyder, his wife, after both worked on productivity software at Microsoft. The startup used AI to analyze workplace writing such as job posts and performance reviews. Harris was Textio’s CTO for nearly eight years, then chief experience officer, before taking over as CEO from Snyder in January 2024. He handed the CEO role to Colleen Gallagher in January 2026 and remains with Textio as founder emeritus.

Textio has raised $42.5 million from investors and went through rounds of layoffs in 2024 and 2025 under Harris. As CEO, he led the launch of Lavalier, an AI-based interview intelligence platform.

Before Textio, Harris spent more than 15 years at Microsoft, where he led the redesign of the Office user interface that produced the Ribbon, and later led user experience for Windows and the touch interface for the original Surface.

After leaving the CEO role at Textio, Harris founded Expedition 60, a firm that helps companies rework how they build software with AI.

“Our pets give us unconditional love, and they deserve the very best in return,” Harris said in a statement, adding that he shares a home with “three very opinionated cats.”

Rover was born at a 2011 Seattle Startup Weekend event, where venture capitalist Greg Gottesman pitched the idea. Aaron Easterly led the company as CEO for 14 years, taking it through the pandemic, a public offering and a $2.3 billion take-private deal with Blackstone in 2024. He stepped down last year and became executive chair, handing the CEO role to Turner.

Rover now operates in 18 countries across North America, Europe and Australia, and says sitters and walkers on its platform have provided 50 million bookings to date. Its brands include cat-sitting marketplaces Meowtel and Cat in a Flat, and Australia-based Mad Paws. Beyond sitting and walking, Rover now offers training in the U.S. and is testing other services.

#5525. Apple Is Reportedly Slashing AI Budgets. Here’s Why Employees Are Worried.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Apple is cutting spending allowances for AI tools.

Even Apple, the most valuable company in the world with a market capitalization of $4.98 trillion, is watching its AI bill.

The tech giant is tightening internal spending limits as it looks to cut costs, Bloomberg reported this week. Apple is reducing how much employees can spend on AI tools to lower costs while simultaneously working to make the technology central to its business.

Some Apple engineers saw their daily AI spending limits fall from $300 to $200 last month, per Bloomberg. The company is considering another reduction that could bring the allowance down to $100 a day for certain engineering groups.

Non-engineering teams also face steep cuts. Apple currently gives these organizations a $100 daily cap for AI use but is considering lowering the limit to as low as $25. Employees who need a higher budget to do their jobs can ask senior executives for an exception.

The spending limits apply to tokens, or the pieces of text and other data that AI models process to complete a request. Providers usually bill according to how many tokens employees use, with more sophisticated AI models typically carrying higher prices. Writing code or processing software can use a substantial amount of tokens.

Apple wants employees to rely more on AI but spend less doing so, according to Bloomberg. The company’s tighter budgets highlight the tension between controlling costs and using AI to overhaul engineering workflows and other internal processes.

The trend isn’t limited to Apple. Across the tech industry, the enthusiasm for letting employees freely experiment with AI is becoming overshadowed by closer oversight of its cost. Companies now have to decide where to cut spending without sacrificing the productivity improvements they hoped to achieve by using the tools.

Bloomberg reported that Apple employees are divided over the lower limits. Some said that the $300 daily budget was more than what most workers needed. Meanwhile, others worried that the cuts signal a wider effort to reduce spending that could eventually result in job cuts.

These concerns have grown as Apple brings in outside consultants to review how the company operates and where it could become more efficient. Bloomberg previously reported in late September that Apple’s new CEO John Ternus, who took over on September 1, wants a faster, leaner organization with fewer layers of management.

Apple’s bills are still climbing despite its internal push to cut costs. The company said this week that its research and development spending rose 32% in fiscal year 2026, reaching $45.8 billion. Higher infrastructure and AI expenses drove the growth.

Other tech giants are also watching their AI spending. In June, Uber limited all employees to $1,500 in monthly token spending. The same month, Meta said it planned to cut employee AI usage by adding token limits. One month later, Tesla informed staff that it would cap employee AI spending at $200 a week.

#5524. Xero CEO: Why America’s entrepreneurship boom is only half the story

Sukhinder Singh Cassidy is the CEO of Xero. Xero and its payroll partner Gusto are both named in this piece, and the owner-pay figure is Gusto data.

One of the most consistent things I hear from founders is some version of: “The business is doing well, so why don’t I feel like I’m winning?”

That question is critical. Because on every headline measure, they are winning. In 2025, the U.S. recorded approximately 5.7 million business applications, a new annual record. This rise was driven by AI, with 60% of new business owners saying they used it to help launch their business that year, double the rate from 12 months earlier.

Small businesses generate trillions in economic activity. They create jobs. They power entire communities. And yet the owner, the person who took the real risk, is asking: Was it really worth it?

We’ve seen this tension before, and speaking from experience, I have felt it. I think about my older sister Nicky, an optometrist who owned a practice in a shopping mall. She worked day and night to make her business succeed, but that stress never fully translated into her bank account. She had the company P&L, but not a framework for understanding whether she was thriving financially or personally.

That gap is what’s hiding in plain sight in the American small business economy right now.

We already measure revenue, job creation, and GDP contribution. These make up the scorecard. And by that scorecard, entrepreneurship looks healthy. But we don’t measure whether the owner is actually earning a living wage.

Data from Xero’s payroll partner Gusto found that in 2025, the median small business owner paid themselves $4,800 per month, about $57,600 per year, in cash wages.

The time investment is even starker. Most small business owners work at least 50 hours a week. Sixty percent work six or more days every week. And our research at Xero shows that owners spend nearly 22 hours a month on finance alone—just tracking and managing money. Success at the business level doesn’t tell you whether success is sustainable for the person living it.

There’s a name for this gap. I call it the Ownership Gap. The hidden side of the small business economy that measures what owners actually get back from everything they put in.

Income matters, obviously. But so do things we don’t track, such as financial resilience, control over your time, access to capital when you need it, or peace of mind when you’ve had a tough month. The confidence that building this business is actually creating a better future for you as the owner, not just for the company’s P&L.

Right now, we ask if the business is working. We rarely ask if business ownership is working for the owner.

This extends to personal wellbeing too. There is a difference between “my business grew” and “my life improved.” A difference between a dream realized and a dream worth realizing. Business success should improve the owner’s life, not quietly consume it.

If business success should be measured by more than growth alone, we need to make the owner’s experience part of the conversation. That starts with listening to owners, understanding the realities they face and the changes they have made in how they run, measure and experience their businesses.

Those stories can spark a broader conversation about whether business growth is creating greater opportunity for the people behind it. A healthier business should be measured by what it produces and what it gives back to the person who built it.

Owners cannot drive this change alone. Policymakers, economists, and investors must rethink how they make decisions.

When all we measure is business output, we optimize for growth without asking whether that growth is sustainable for the people creating it. We celebrate record business formation without asking what kind of livelihoods those businesses actually create. We see higher small business revenue and assume owners are doing better—when in reality, they might be working harder for the same return or lesser return.

This shapes lending decisions. It shapes the support programs we fund. It shapes how we think about entrepreneurship itself.

The fix isn’t complicated. It’s not about replacing the metrics we already use. It’s about completing the picture. Adding owner health metrics alongside business health as a measure of entrepreneurial success.

This starts by asking different questions. When business formation rises, ask what kinds of income those businesses are generating. When small business sales grow, ask whether owners have greater financial resilience. Create space for data that disaggregates by business type and owner circumstances. Build frameworks that let business owners connect what their business is earning to what they’re actually taking home.

Then make that data visible with the wider business community. Right now, we’re flying blind on owner outcomes. We can see the business is thriving. We can’t see if the engine underneath is actually healthy.

I’ve always believed that collective growth and individual reward go hand in hand. We need to help small business owners globally understand what ownership actually delivers. Not just in revenue, but in resilience, security, time, and wellbeing. This starts with changing what we measure. Owners should look beyond revenue and growth to what their businesses return to them personally as well.

For policymakers, business leaders and economists, the ask is to broaden the definition of a healthy small-business economy beyond output and revenue. Put owners at the center of research, public debate and policy, and measure whether business success is improving their lives.

In short, owners will help rewrite the scorecard. The wider ecosystem needs to start using it.

We have a record number of people building businesses in different countries around the world. In this new Owner Economy, let’s make sure we’re actually measuring whether it’s working out for them. Because a healthy small business economy isn’t one where the business thrives and the owner burns out. It’s one where both succeed together over the short, medium and long term by measuring all the metrics that matter.

#5523. After Elizabeth Holmes Ate His Product, Everything Changed for His Business: ‘This Publicity, It’s in the Millions of Dollars’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Ricky Hirsch, founder of Think Jerky, was “overwhelmed” when his brand appeared on screen.

On October 16, Ricky Hirsch’s meat snack startup Think Jerky experienced an unscripted marketing moment so crazy it’s “not even once in a lifetime,” the founder and CEO tells Entrepreneur.

Hirsch launched Think Jerky in 2015, building on his finance background and creative inclinations to start a “cool” jerky brand with a minimalist design and unique, chef-crafted flavors.

The brand’s sriracha honey flavor, created by Michelin-starred and two-time James Beard Award-winning chef Gale Gand, landed in the spotlight last month.

Hirsch was watching poker on television at his home in Austin, Texas, when he received a text from one of his employees.

She was in New York and had just attended a screening of You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s A24 meta-documentary featuring Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the lead-up to her federal prison sentence.

Holmes was convicted of one count of conspiracy alongside three wire fraud charges stemming from more than $140 million in investor losses in 2022.

“ I was familiar with Elizabeth Holmes,” Hirsch says. “I’m in the business world, so that always intrigued me. And I saw the Hulu series. I was not familiar with Nathan Fielder at all.”

Hirsch’s employee was “freaking out” over Think Jerky’s cameo, the founder recalls.

In You Can See Everything, Holmes requests turkey jerky from the prison vending machine. The scene is reenacted with Amanda Seyfried, who plays Holmes in Hulu’s The Dropout. At one point, the camera pans to the vending machine — “it’s like product placement, the best, most beautiful shot,” Hirsch says.

The film ends with Holmes and her husband Billy Evans eating Think Jerky.

Hirsch decided to see the film for himself the next day, but he still had no idea how much the on-screen moment would change his business. “I brought some jerky with me,” Hirsch says. “And when it came on screen, I was overwhelmed. I was like, This is wild.”

The founder walked out of the theater in Austin with about 30 bags of jerky in tow. He started handing them out to people — and they “were freaking out.” It was a sign of things to come.

Within two weeks, Think Jerky’s honey sriracha sales were up 345% on the company’s website and 92% on Amazon. Someone posted on X that the Texas supermarket chain H-E-B had sold out of “the Elizabeth Holmes jerky.”

Reddit forums dissected what Think Jerky might represent as a narrative symbol. (“They think it symbolizes manipulation or control. There’s all these theories”). Fans dressed up as the Think Jerky bag for Halloween (“You have to make that costume”). YouTube videos discussed it. Restaurants reached out for collaborations. People hawked fake merchandise.

“If somebody wanted to pay for this publicity, it’s in the millions of dollars,” Hirsch says.

Hirsch chalks up some of the virality to how the brand’s name — “Think” Jerky — plays right into the “wild,” layered film and becomes its own sort of small character.

Now, the founder is determined to add as much fuel to the marketing fire as possible.

But that’s a tall order for a fully bootstrapped company with four employees. “People are stepping up, our significant others are stepping up and all that, but we are not a big business,” Hirsch says. “We do not have a big team. We never raised money, which is very unique in my industry.”

Hirsch acknowledges that people might not remember Think Jerky’s logo or company name in five years, but they might remember the shot of that bag. So he’s doing his best to make it a meme and keep the conversation going.

The team is going to San Diego for the Food & Wine festival. Gale Gand will make an egg dish (another humorous nod to the film) and top it with the jerky. The team is also planning lookalike contests, where they’ll hand out jerky and display a cutout of Holmes.

Sales remain strong, and Hirsch anticipates selling out. Think Jerky has about 60 days’ worth of finished inventory in reserve to meet the demand.

Currently, the brand is revamping its website, which will be complete in about a month, for a “soft rebrand” that fully captures the product’s chef-crafted approach. Think Jerky is also launching new products, including a Thanksgiving turkey stick made with four-time James Beard Award-winner Andrew Zimmern.

Looking ahead, Hirsch would be very interested in raising money for Think Jerky with the right partner. “ If Daniel Lubetzky wants to talk to me, I would love to talk to Daniel Lubetzky,” the founder says.

Hirsch is excited to continue leaning into Think Jerky’s surprise breakout and explosive growth.

“ I thought it was going fade maybe, after the third weekend, but it’s growing,” Hirsch says. “People are reaching out, people want to collaborate. I want to introduce my creative marketing and hopefully bring our company to a new level.”

On October 16, Ricky Hirsch’s meat snack startup Think Jerky experienced an unscripted marketing moment so crazy it’s “not even once in a lifetime,” the founder and CEO tells Entrepreneur.

Hirsch launched Think Jerky in 2015, building on his finance background and creative inclinations to start a “cool” jerky brand with a minimalist design and unique, chef-crafted flavors.

The brand’s sriracha honey flavor, created by Michelin-starred and two-time James Beard Award-winning chef Gale Gand, landed in the spotlight last month.

#5522. Finpilot raises $10M for AI agents that handle the grunt work for institutional investors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:04 am

Seattle startup Finpilot, which uses AI agents to take the paperwork off the plates of people who invest money for hospitals, pension funds and foundations, has raised $10 million in a Series A round.

The round was led by Bay Area venture firm Lobby Capital, with participation from Madrona, which led Finpilot’s $4 million seed round in 2024. Finpilot, which has raised about $14.5 million since its 2023 founding, plans to use the new funding to expand its product and hire across the company.

Its customers include in-house investment teams at institutions and firms that manage money on their behalf. In the industry, they’re known as allocators, because they spread capital across outside fund managers. Much of their information arrives from fund managers as PDFs and spreadsheets, and someone has to read the reports, pull out the numbers and enter them into the right systems.

Finpilot pulls that information into one place and has its agents handle much of the work. The idea is to let investment teams spend their time on judgment and decisions, not on reading data from documents and typing it into a database, said Lakshay Chauhan, Finpilot’s co-founder and CEO, in an interview.

“Nobody wakes up like, ‘All right, I’m excited to do that,'” he said.

It’s a change of course for the company. When GeekWire covered its seed round, Finpilot was building a ChatGPT-style tool for analysts researching public companies. It shifted to allocators in mid-2024, Chauhan said, after concluding that AI added only marginal value in public markets, where Bloomberg and S&P Capital IQ had already organized most of the data.

“There’s no Bloomberg for what they do,” he said of allocators.

Customers include Seattle Children’s, Children’s Health in Dallas, Hackensack Meridian Health in New Jersey, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Wyoming, the Wyoming Retirement System, outsourced investment firm TIFF, and Seattle wealth management firm Laird Norton Wetherby. Some of those institutions hadn’t changed their core systems in 15 years, Chauhan said.

Finpilot has about 28 institutional customers in all, and revenue has grown tenfold since the start of the year, he said. It hasn’t lost a customer yet, he noted.

How it works: Finpilot pulls an institution’s data from its portfolio management system, document storage and other sources into a single record, matching each fund, holding and client to one identifier. Users ask questions in a chat window and set up agents to handle recurring work.

In an example Chauhan described, an agent could review updates from 35 private equity managers at the end of a quarter, figure out what changed and point an analyst to the three things that need attention. Agents also prepare briefings before meetings with fund managers, and they ask a person for approval when a step needs one.

Some customers run Finpilot alongside their existing software. Others have used it to replace older customer relationship management and research management systems, where investment teams log their dealings with fund managers.

Chauhan said Finpilot most often gets compared with general-purpose AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, including finance-focused versions like Claude for Financial Services, and with legacy CRM vendors.

Chauhan said the difference is accuracy. A 10-page report from a chatbot has to be checked number by number before it goes to a chief investment officer. In Finpilot, every number links back to the document it came from, so it can be checked.

In finance, he said, “you cannot be wrong.”

Finpilot runs its own in-house model for the high-volume job of reading financial documents, and uses models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google for other tasks. It doesn’t train AI models on customer data and keeps each customer’s data separate, Chauhan said.

Founders: Chauhan grew up in India and came to the U.S. for a master’s degree in aerospace engineering. He interned at Boeing in Seattle, but when he graduated, he said, many full-time aerospace jobs required U.S. citizenship or permanent residency, and he was in the country on a visa.

He went to work for an engineering optimization software company and studied quantitative investing on the side. That led him to a paper by John Alberg, co-founder of Seattle investment firm Euclidean Technologies, which uses machine learning to pick stocks. Chauhan called Alberg repeatedly to propose working together, and Alberg eventually hired him. Chauhan later led AI at Euclidean.

Alberg is Finpilot’s co-founder and executive chairman but isn’t involved in day-to-day operations. His late father, Tom Alberg, co-founded Madrona.

Finpilot has about 14 employees, up from four in 2024. All are based in Seattle except one in Boise, Idaho. The company recently moved into the AGC Building on Lake Union after outgrowing its old office.

What’s next: Finpilot plans to fill six or seven jobs in the next few months, in product, marketing, client success, sales and business development, and about as many early next year.

Part of the money will go to implementation teams, Chauhan said. Their job is to sit down with each customer, learn how its investment team works and show it how to redo that work with AI agents.

#5521. Bullying rates reach 68% at some colleges, on par with emergency services — and students angling for better grades are the biggest source

Faculty and university staff members report being bullied in two ways: by their colleagues and supervisors, and by their students over grades, according to an international study I conducted with colleagues Zahra Moradi and Deborah Circo.

Researchers define workplace bullying as harmful acts of mistreatment between people that go beyond incivility and cross the line to intentionally cause harm. In other words, it’s behavior any reasonable person would know isn’t OK.

Junior faculty and staff faced more workplace bullying from peers. Faculty members and staff who are Black, Indigenous or people of color were targeted more frequently.

Senior faculty were more likely than younger educators to report being bullied by students over grades. Although bullying usually runs down the chain of power – for example, from a boss to an employee – grade bullying flips that. Researchers call it contrapower harassment – when someone with less formal power targets someone with more.

More than 30% of adult workers in the U.S. and Canada experience bullying, harassment and sexual abuse in the workplace at any given time, harming both individuals and organizations.

That rate is more than double in academia, where bullying rates are as high as 68% at some institutions, far exceeding those in general workplaces and aligning with high-stress fields like emergency services, according to our peer-reviewed findings published in the October 2026 Journal of Multidisciplinary Research and Practice.

Academic bullying undermines both the well-being of staff and faculty and the integrity of higher education institutions.

Thirty percent of our survey respondents reported that students pressured them for a better grade. Students’ tactics included threatening grade appeals, malicious complaints, negative online reviews, emotional manipulation and intimidation. Women and minority faculty are particularly affected. Over time, the bullying creates a toxic environment that damages relationships between faculty and students and hurts the quality of education for everyone.

Such pressure could result in mental health issues like anxiety and depression, decreased job satisfaction and reduced productivity. These dynamics not only affect individual faculty members but can also lead to long-term damage to the reputation of institutions and negatively impact students’ educational experiences.

We surveyed 189 faculty and staff at colleges and universities in Canada, the U.S. and U.K.

Anonymous respondents reported how often they’d faced 22 common forms of mistreatment from colleagues and supervisors. A separate set of questions asked about pressure from students over grades.

The most common issues related to colleagues weren’t shouting or threats. They were easier to dismiss: unmanageable workloads, withheld information and impossible deadlines.

Pressure from students over grades was reported more frequently than bullying from colleagues.

Gaps remain in understanding the root causes of bullying of faculty.

Studies that follow the same faculty over several years could show how grade bullying builds over time, and whether it pushes people to leave or lose trust in their institutions. One likely pattern is that grade bullying escalates when it works, wearing faculty down until they either give in or leave their jobs.

Researchers need to test what actually works to stop bullying, and whether those fixes hold up at different kinds of colleges and universities.

Bigger studies would help. So would sitting down with faculty and hearing their experiences in their own words to add context that a survey can’t capture.

Future research could also explore interventions to mitigate bullying and measure their effectiveness across diverse educational contexts.

Bullying at work is a form of violence. The harm is psychological rather than physical, but it’s real. Change starts with higher standards of conduct for everyone, from first-year students to senior administrators and leaders committed to enforcing respectful rules.

The Research Brief is a short take on interesting academic work.

Jason Walker, Associate Professor of Psychology, Health and Wellness, Adler University
